abstractText:
It is essential that robots working side-by-side with people be able to offer physical assistance.  However, robots do not yet take the initiative to help. Instead, they typically follow preset plans for collaboration, or respond only when users explicitly ask for help.  While useful in many situations, this reactive approach is poorly suited for many collaborative applications. This project focuses on enabling robots to proactively offer physical assistance that is timely, task-appropriate, and wanted by their human partners.  The goal is to construct robots that can answer three key questions: (1) Does a teammate need help? (2) Can I (or someone else) help? and (3) Should I help?  By enabling these capabilities, this project will make collaborative human-robot teams function more fluently and efficiently. 

To develop these capabilities, three research thrusts that are naturally intertwined but that capture important computational aspects of these tasks, will be advanced. First, perceiving other agents through a Theory of Mind for robots. The research team will develop computational models derived from our understanding of how humans represent the knowledge, beliefs, and desires of others to maintain context-sensitive models of the mental states of human and robotic teammates.  Second, planning for supportive actions.  The team will construct a system that generates possible supportive actions that the robot could take to help a teammate by using a trained model of the robot's own capabilities along with a predictive planning system that determines if these actions have value to the team.  Third, decision making within the dynamics of a group. The robot will monitor and engage in social activities that support the overall dynamics of its partners including both conventional conversational interfaces and more subtle social mechanisms that facilitate collaboration.

abstractText:
Despite the incredible success of Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems, their predictions and decisions have been shown to discriminatory in crucial domains such as employment, housing, and lending. Hence, it is imperative to center the interests of the public, protect disadvantaged groups, and empower society in the design and execution of the technology we create. This can only be done by considering the entire ecosystem in which the AI is situated – one cannot assume perfect data or perfect usage of the technology. In this project novel approaches towards anti-discriminatory AI will be assessed and redesigned taking into account common flaws in the data stream. The evaluation of the systems will be done in the broader context in which the technology is commonly used in order to assess the downstream effects and long-term impacts of different approaches to fair machine learning interventions. Further, the researchers will produce engaging content for students, the AI community and the public, in order to engage all in working towards the socially-conscious design of AI systems.

From a technical standpoint, this work will design new approaches that take into account the problems that arise when a machine-learning algorithm is lifted out of the lab and placed into a broader ecosystem in which data is erroneous and humans interact with the AI system. Outcomes of this project will include new models and algorithms for fundamental problems in fair machine learning such as classification, summarization, ranking, and online advertising that can satisfy fairness demands while simultaneously performing well according to their original objectives. Importantly, these algorithms will function in a robust manner that account for realities such as missing, incorrect, or adversarial data. The projects will increase our understanding of the demand and nature of fairness within specific social and economic contexts, and the impact that fair machine learning interventions can have. This project will significantly impact and advance the technical core of computer and data science, and inculcate a more holistic approach towards social justice in AI systems.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

abstractText:
Biological systems are inherently complex. Increasingly sophisticated technologies are
being used in biomedical science in order to make sense of this complexity and to understand the
underlying factors that cause disease. These technologies generate vast amounts of data in many
different forms, from changes in how genes and proteins are expressed in individual cells over time,
to detailed clinical imaging data on large patient populations and whole genome sequencing studies
across hundreds of thousands of people. These newly developed datatypes could help uncover
important mechanisms and pathways that underpin health and disease. However, there is a large
gap between the information contained in these datasets and the ability to extract meaningful
insights. Here the PI proposes to address this by developing new machine learning approaches based
on mathematical foundations that will allow us to make sense of these complex datasets. The PI will develop deep representation learning techniques that focus on gaining overall insight into the
structures, dynamics, interactions, and predictive features of the data, and will allow 
specific hypotheses regarding the underlying regulatory mechanisms that drive disease in different
contexts to derived. The proposal will also involve training a postdoc, graduate student, and mentorship of local high school students. In addition, it will enable the development of an online workshop to
widely disseminate knowledge of unsupervised data analysis to a diverse array of participants from
across the country.

This project proposes to advance biomedical data analysis via three main thrusts. The first thrust is focused on forming deep multiscale representations of the data based on data geometry, graph signal processing, and topological concepts, in combination with powerful, deep learning systems. Such representations will allow for exploration of structure and meaningful, predictive abstractions of the data in a scalable fashion. Our second thrust is focused on integrating multiple modalities of data and organizing multitudes of related datasets using optimal transport and generative models to gain insight into entire cohorts of patients or perturbation conditions. Our third thrust is focused on learning high dimensional stochastic dynamics of the data using neural SDE (stochastic differential equation) and graph ODE (ordinary differential equation) networks to gain insight into underlying gene regulatory networks. We apply our approaches in the context of several specific biomedical challenges. Achieving these aims will enable integration and exploration of a large volume of data for explaining underlying regulatory mechanisms and dynamic phenotypic changes.

abstractText:
The last two decades have witnessed enormous increase in wireless data transfer, impacting every aspect our lives and our nation's economy. This has led to a spectrum crunch in frequency bands below 6 GHz that are the most useful for intermediate and long-range wireless communications. Even as new spectrum is allocated for different wireless networks and systems, satisfying the increasing demand of high data rates will lead to coexistence of active users (that generate signals) and passive users (that sense signals for weather sensing, astronomy, and other applications). Inevitably, interference occurs when these users share the same frequency band or when active users operate in bands close to that used by passive users. Therefore, there is a critical need for an approach to efficiently manage and reduce such interference, which will allow for further improved spectrum usage. This project will address this challenge and focus on a cross-layer software-hardware approach for spectrum coexistence with rapid interferer learning, detection, and mitigation (SHIELD). On a societal scale, the proposed research can improve spectrum utilization and increase access to in-demand wireless data without adversely impacting existing users, which will have direct economic impact. The broader impacts also include major outreach activities involving high school students and aiming at broadening the participation of women and underrepresented minorities, as well as incorporation of new hardware, software, and network architecture into undergraduate and graduate classes.

Specifically, this interdisciplinary project will bridge the gap between the broad areas of integrated circuits, communications, networking, and machine learning, and will focuses on enabling rapid interferer learning, detection, and mitigation for spectrum coexistence based on the co-design of novel RF hardware and network control architecture. The main activities include: (i) extensive spectrum measurements and data collection for characterizing the spectrum usage and properties of potential interferers, (ii) development of a novel reconfigurable 0.4-4.0 GHz MIMO receiver architecture leveraging a concurrent auxiliary receiver for rapid interference detection and N-path sequence-mixing for nulling specific interferers, and (iii) design of an intelligent control plane, which integrates software-defined networking and machine learning techniques, for efficient spectrum monitoring, management, and resource allocation across spatially distributed receivers. The developed hardware and software will be evaluated in the lab setting and in real-world environments through their integration in a city-scale wireless testbed.

projectOutComesReport:
As the number of wireless users and applications continues to grow, the radio frequency spectrum–particularly in the sub-7 GHz bands–has become increasingly congested. This congestion leads to significant co-channel and adjacent-channel interference, degrading performance and reliability for both incumbent and emerging systems. There is, therefore, a critical need for intelligent wireless systems capable of rapidly detecting, identifying, and mitigating interference in dynamic spectral environments. This project addressed this challenge through a tightly integrated software-hardware approach for rapid interferer detection and mitigation. We developed intelligent wireless receiver architectures that incorporate adaptive control mechanisms and machine learning (ML) frameworks to enable real-time spectrum awareness and decision-making. In addition, we designed and evaluated advanced spectrum coexistence strategies that enhance interoperability between heterogeneous active communication systems. Together, these contributions provide a foundation for more resilient, spectrum-efficient wireless networks in increasingly crowded environments.

On the hardware side, we developed and demonstrated: (i) A new class of ultra-low-power reconfigurable receivers and analog correlators in low-cost commercial CMOS technologies. Our receiver architecture achieved state-of-the-art sensitivity and interferer tolerance while maintaining high integration and low power consumption. Subsequent work extended this foundation to higher-order reconfigurable filtering in 14 nm CMOS. (ii) A major technical breakthrough was the development of a fully analog correlator architecture capable of direct-RF processing at multi-GS/s rates. A correlator is a basic building block that computes the correlation or similarity between two signals. It is used in several signal processing applications and is of interest for machine learning as well. We achieved state-of-the-art low power consumption for analog correlators and subsequently demonstrated multi-lag cross-correlators exceeding 1000 TOPS/W, with significant compute density improvements. These results showed that high-speed correlation, traditionally performed digitally, can be executed directly in the analog/RF domain with substantial energy savings.

On the software and algorithm side, we developed: (i) Energy-efficient and protocol-aware spectrum monitoring and sensing algorithms for Wi-Fi and 5G networks, experimentally validated using a software-defined radio (SDR) testbed. Specifically, for Wi-Fi networks, we leverage the unique structure of the long training field (LTF) such that various Wi-Fi packet properties can be detected and estimated using a receiver operating at sub-Nyquist sampling that is much smaller than the Wi-Fi signal bandwidth. For 5G networks, we leverage uplink resource grids to extract radar signals through radar signal separation, resource grid reshaping, and zero-shot template correlation based on a portable model trained purely on synthetic data.

(ii) An open-source framework, Geo2SigMap, for constructing scalable and high-fidelity wireless digital twins from publicly available geospatial data such as OpenStreetMap and the USGS Lidar Point Cloud. Geo2SigMap also introduces an ML model for efficient signal coverage estimation that can be trained on purely synthetic data and inferred using sparse observations, which is then experimentally validated using large-scale, real-world CBRS measurements.

(iii) A multi-channel programmable radio platform, SPEAR, for wideband radio and spectrum applications based on the Xilinx RFSoC ZCU216 board. SPEAR supports real-time streaming of up to 1.2 GHz aggregated bandwidth across 2T2R, 4T4R, 8T8R, or 16T16R configurations, and features a Python-based software stack and multi-tile synchronization (MTS) capability to achieve deterministic, high-speed data transfer between the memory and analog/digital data converters across up to 16 TX and 16 RX channels.

(iv) Distributed scheduling and sectorization algorithms, and network slicing policies for wireless networks with provable performance guarantees such as throughout optimality across the extended capacity region.

Research results have been broadly disseminated through publications at leading venues spanning circuits (ISSCC, JSSC), dynamic spectrum sharing (DySPAN), wireless communications (ICC, MILCOM), and networking (MobiHoc, INFOCOM, TON). In addition to peer-reviewed publications, we have released open-source software frameworks and measurement datasets, including Geo2SigMap and SPEAR, to promote reproducibility, community benchmarking, and broader adoption of the project’s technical advances. These open resources have enabled other researchers and practitioners to build upon our spectrum modeling, sensing, and coexistence methodologies. Beyond academic dissemination, the project team has actively engaged with leading industry stakeholders to explore pathways for technology readiness and impacts on real-world deployment.

abstractText:
Society is having a hard time governing digital systems, and poorly governed systems lead to gaps in society's willingness to trust these systems with sensitive or high-priority tasks. Part of this challenge arises from the fact that law and software address rules and behavior at very different levels of detail. Laws must be general in their application and thus leave interpretation and detailed requirements to the discretion of software developers. This leaves software developers, who cannot be expected to be legal experts, having to decide what is the proper technical design to comply with often-complex legal rules. For example, when a privacy law such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) requires that users have a right to delete their data, does that mean all data, including backups? Without clear answers to such questions, developers can’t be confident that they have successfully complied with legal requirements, and then the public who uses these systems has little reason to trust them. This project's novelties are to introduce design patterns that help software developers assemble components reliably and purposefully, in the knowledge that they meet policy requirements effectively and thus warrant the confidence of the public. The project's impact benefits society in two ways. First, by closing the abstraction gap between law and systems, methods and tools developed in this project help software developers build systems that comply with legal obligations. Second, the project furthers the development of a research community in computer science and law. 

The LAChS (pronounced "lox") project makes two contributions toward better understanding of how to build accountable software systems. First, policy concepts allow software developers to identify the functional aspects of systems they are developing in order to assess whether the functions of the system are consistent with the policy constraints associated with the computations they are performing. Along with policy concepts, the project introduces policy standards -- functional descriptions of the requirements of law. Together, policy concepts and policy standards provide a software-engineering framework through which developers can more easily build systems that are accountable to legal requirements. Second, the project develops an integrated legal-technical methodology for assessing the accountability properties of a system with respect to a set of legal requirements. Prior work has generally sought to define accountability solely as a property of information systems. The project shows that a full understanding of accountability requires considering the properties of both law and computing systems. In sum, this research is premised on the view that, with respect to key societal priorities such as privacy, the law has actually made considerable progress in defining key rights for the digital, while underlying technology is still struggling to adapt to these challenges. Thus the project aims to bring more clear abstraction, modularization and composability to legal and technical methodologies in order to better meet these challenges.

abstractText:
As society is becoming more and more dependent on software systems, questions arise about how such software can be developed responsibly. In the design of software systems, flexibility and innovation must be balanced with safeguarding the public. Regulators who design policy to steward software’s effect on society often have a hard time capturing clear guidance to hold software systems accountable and keeping up with new technologies, such as the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI). Software engineers have often been left with vague guidance and no measurable goals, such as the EU’s “right to explanation.” While clarifying guidance or court decisions may eventually provide more actionable details, policy implementation is a slow, reactive process that can delay adoption of improvements. To reconcile software and policy design and construct a proactive policy framework for accountable software systems, guidance for qualities such as explainability, safety, and fairness requires more attention.

This project will investigate cross-domain principles for policy design, setting corresponding obligations for software engineers, particularly in the context of AI-supported systems. Results will help stakeholders to deliberately design policy with evidence-based guidance for a specific domain. The project will facilitate interactions between policy makers and software engineers in understanding capabilities and societal expectations toward forming policy goals, investigate policy dimensions and the concrete tradeoffs involved, and connect the policy to specific quality-assurance obligations that could be used in a regulatory evaluation covering both AI and non-AI parts of the system. Specifically, the project will first investigate the important dimensions for policy design (e.g., strictness of regulation, level of evidence, policy specificity) using stakeholder interviews, historical analysis, and technical analysis. It then will evaluate, with several experiments, how design decisions affect outcomes, interact with each other, and result in tradeoffs -- which will be encoded and validated as policy design patterns. The research will combine multiple research methods, including interviews, literature and document analyses, controlled experiments, prototyping, and writer’s workshops. It will deeply integrate social-science research on policy design and regulation with software-engineering research on system design and quality assurance. The research will be disseminated broadly across multiple communities and through engagement with regulators. Educational material will be developed for multiple courses and shared publicly.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern AI-enabled systems are increasingly governed not only by technical performance requirements but also by policy expectations around accountability, transparency, and explainability. Yet policy statements are often either too abstract to guide engineering practice or too prescriptive to remain valid as technology changes. This project investigated cross-domain principles for policy design, drawing on cases in cancer imaging, educational games, and consumer recommender applications. Our goal was to understand how different stakeholders interpret societal expectations and to develop policy design mechanisms for accountability that (1) set future-proof goals, (2) provide practical guidance for regulators and software engineers, and (3) remain flexible enough to evolve. A central theme was connecting policy goals to concrete quality assurance obligations and evidence that can be evaluated in regulatory or organizational review—covering both AI components and the surrounding non-AI software and processes. The overall goal is to improve accountability for software projects through shaping their engineering practices.

 

Intellectual merit. The project produced multiple complementary research contributions. We analyzed the outcomes of a policy design experiment (initiated via an REU project) and identified nine empirical observations and three recommendations for how to run effective policy design projects. A key insight is that sustained interdisciplinary engagement—rather than one-off consultations—can produce higher-quality, implementable policies, and that this model can be scaled when less-experienced practitioners are guided by experts and supported through research programs. Subsequently, we conducted four iterations of a controlled experiment with over 300 participants examining how developers respond to policy requirements for explanations in the context of an AI-powered medical device (namely, a screening tool for diabetic retinopathy). Unlike many short studies, participants engaged for roughly eight hours each, enabling deeper measurement of how policy framing affects the global and local explanations developers design, the harms they identify, and the tradeoffs they make. In a nutshell, we found that developers without dedicated training struggle to interpret policy and conceptualize evidence; they largely write explanations in an intuitive fashion, ignoring specific policy requirements and user needs. We show that better tooling and educational interventions can help to shape developer actions more effectively when combined with policy. Third, we generated a conceptual bridge between machine-learning explainability and the regulated practice of informed consent in medicine—two contexts that require communicating complex concepts under strong knowledge asymmetry—deriving design lessons and cautions from decades of practice and critique. Finally, we addressed a practical barrier to accountability work: many practitioners view responsible AI processes as irrelevant or bureaucratic. We developed LLM-based tooling to generate short, context-relevant “sticky stories” about ML harms and showed in a controlled experiment that these narratives broaden harm identification and deepen reflection, complementing explainability and accountability efforts.

 

Broader impacts. The project's broader impacts include explicit suggestions for policy makers, regulators, and engineering teams to align on realistic accountability expectations and on what evidence is needed to evaluate AI-enabled products in practice. We disseminated results through peer-reviewed publications (including ICSE, FAccT, AIES, CHI) and widely used public course materials, and we actively engaged communities beyond our home disciplines. Findings were presented at venues spanning computer science and social science, including FAccT, ICSE, the Eastern Sociological Society meeting, the Society for the Social Studies of Science, and the American Sociological Association. We also delivered invited talks and keynotes to reach cross-disciplinary and practitioner audiences: a keynote at CAIN 2024 (AI Engineering), invited talks at the Symposium on Model Accountability, Sustainability and Healthcare (SMASH) 2025, the Yale School of Medicine, Smith College, and Columbia University’s Sociology of Algorithms group, as well as presentations to organizations and practitioner communities such as the Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning and GE Healthcare. The project trained graduate students, undergraduate research assistants, and multiple REU students in qualitative methods, controlled experimentation, policy analysis, and communication of findings to the public. It also shaped education for large cohorts of future engineers through integration into technical and sociological courses, influenced instruction at multiple universities via openly shared materials, and contributed to new interdisciplinary curricula and textbook development efforts.

abstractText:
The field of biology has seen dramatic advances in the past two decades, both in its research findings and research methodology. Vision and Change (V&C) in undergraduate biology education began nearly fifteen years ago with conversations in the biological sciences community about how those advances challenge the nature of what students ought to learn in their undergraduate programs of study. This project aims to serve the national interest by undertaking a holistic evaluation of the Vision and Change “movement” to better demonstrate how it has contributed (and continues to contribute) to improving undergraduate biology education. The project will provide an organizing structure by identifying short-, mid-, and long-term V&C outcomes and connecting them in a way that affords stakeholders a useful and helpful way to “see” the successes, opportunities, and future trajectory of V&C.  The project will develop a visual and easy-to-understand theoretical framework known as a Pathway Model of V&C. The V&C Pathway Model is a visualization that will be developed through the systematic integration of the literature on V&C as well as key stakeholder perspectives on what V&C is and how it works. The project will enable the V&C community to develop a stronger understanding of what their impact has been on undergraduate biology and what they should turn their attention to in upcoming years to maximize the impact.

The project aims to develop a theoretical framework that will: a) organize and articulate the wide variety of V&C activities and outcomes; b) consolidate the current body of knowledge about the nature and extent of V&C's use and impact; and c) structure future directions for V&C evaluation at both the local and national levels. The model will strive to 1) identify and address critical assumptions underlying implementation of V&C; b) optimize plans for implementing V&C at all levels; c) enable local implementers to strategically focus their evaluation efforts; and d) provide national-level investigators with an organizing guide for their research. Once the initial theoretical model is developed, the content of the model will be validated through the contributions of three V&C stakeholder cohorts via online focus group sessions. These include early V&C organizers, current V&C implementers, and organization- and system-level change-makers. The project will develop a five-year plan for expanding adoption of the V&C framework. The five-year plan will be distributed alongside the pathway model as a credible tool for planning, decision-making, and evaluation. Subsequently, the pathway model will be used in a series of webinars as a training and brainstorming tool to inform a wider range of stakeholders on the V&C principles and outcomes. Through focused dissemination efforts this project has the potential to enrich the national conversation around V&C. This project is funded by the Division of Undergraduate Education’s Improving Undergraduate STEM Education Program through its Program Description 21-7412 that calls for projects that study the impact of the V&C movement in Undergraduate Biology Education.

projectOutComesReport:
Summary: The Vision & Change (V&C) movement in undergraduate biology education has motivated and guided instructors for over a decade. Individual components of V&C, such as active learning, have been well-researched. The movement, however, has been difficult to evaluate. This difficulty stems from the evolving definition of V&C and variable implementation of V&C across institutional contexts. This study investigated V&C’s theory of change through leveraging an evaluation approach known as pathway modeling. This approach involves consolidating the V&C literature and conducting focus groups with key V&C stakeholders. Specifically, we first represented the current body of knowledge about V&C in a visual model depicting the connections between the movement’s activities and outcomes. We then confirmed and analyzed the pathway model through iterative literature reviews and focus groups held with key V&C stakeholders. Findings from this process confirmed the effectiveness of active learning and undergraduate research in improving student outcomes. They also highlighted areas where V&C can be further developed, including student-instructor relationships, accessibility and relevance of the curriculum, local-level assessment, departmental and institutional support, and retention and career preparation. We also identified and documented assessment tools that evaluate V&C activities and outcomes based on these areas, informing specific strategies for optimizing key outcomes from V&C implementation. Ultimately, this study offers guidance on how V&C’s current successes can be leveraged and how the field may envision a V&C 2.0 to support student success. 

Broader Impacts: Through dissemination, this project enriched the national conversation around V&C by developing a pathway model representing the theory of change underlying the movement. While the long-term outcomes of V&C have been well-documented in previous reports and publications, the mechanisms in which these outcomes are achieved are less known. This project addresses this gap by investigating the components and immediate outcomes that lead to these longer-term outcomes. Findings have been shared across various channels reaching the undergraduate STEM education community and with key V&C stakeholders participating in this work, including early-organizers, current implementers, and organizational change makers. This dissemination has positioned and promoted the final developed pathway model as a credible tool for planning, decision-making, and evaluation for effective undergraduate biology reform. Collectively this project contributes to a better understanding of how the V&C community (and undergraduate STEM at large) has impacted biology education and where they should turn their attention to maximize impact.  

Intellectual Merit: By consolidating knowledge about V&C from the research literature and stakeholder feedback into a visual pathway model, this project positions the V&C community to better evaluate the movement’s impact, identifying successes and areas for development. Indeed, pathway models have been increasingly applied within the context of undergraduate STEM education to effectively monitor and evaluate ongoing efforts to improve outcomes for students and faculty. In the short-term, the pathway model and project insights provide the V&C community with knowledge about how the current body of evidence supports important V&C outcomes, how local-level efforts support longer-term outcomes, and how current efforts may shift their focus based on these insights. In the long-term, the final pathway model provides an evidence-based, visual framework that the V&C community can use to systemically guide and organize their inquiry. With this organizing structure, monitoring and evaluating of current V&C initiatives can become more effective and impactful. V&C practitioners, researchers, and evaluators also receive a cache of resources, including a visually organized set of measures, relevant research articles, and stakeholder feedback that can deepen their understanding of V&C.

abstractText:
A global-scale public infrastructure of distributed computing resources, in the form of data centers of various scales, has emerged in the past decade. Today, a user of this global infrastructure must trust the infrastructure vendors based on their informal textual contracts.  This trust model provides limited legal protection of user interests and has become a key barrier for more services to migrate into the public infrastructure, stymieing innovation and competition.  This project's key novelty is to build highly performant, certified execution environments (CEEs) for large-scale distributed systems. In doing so, the project explores, refines, and discovers design principles for scaling certified trust --- specifically, scaling up to include the entire software stack, and scaling out to include globally distributed resources.  The project's main impact is to enable and promote trustworthy, performant, cost-effective uses of the public global infrastructure, empowering applications and services for a global market. Specifically it will lower the barrier of entrance for startups to enter a global market and as a result, foster competition and innovation, and make information technologies more accessible. It is intended to profoundly change many industries that traditionally heavily rely on proprietary IT infrastructures, e.g., mobile networks. 

The project makes three related scientific contributions. First, it contributes new technologies for building distributed CEE enclaves for running global-scale applications. CEEs extend remote attestation (as in trusted execution environments (TEEs)) with formal verification so the chain of trust can be used to establish not only the authenticity of enclave binaries but also the trustworthiness properties. Second, it provides hardware and software support to accelerate the underlying mechanisms for isolation, integrity, and confidentiality. These themes range from support for better isolation to CPUs and TEEs, but also include fast mechanisms for emerging hardware accelerators. Finally, the team of researchers explores the extension of certifiably trustworthy execution environments to emerging disaggregated datacenter designs using a software-defined-network-based decomposition of functionalities. The insights gleaned from their study guide the development of new algorithm-driven, data structure-driven, and hardware-driven solutions for the trustworthy disaggregated cloud design. During the Planning stage, the investigators are developing a prototype testbed to evaluate the feasibility of building a high-performance trustworthy global-scale mobile network using cloud-scale disaggregated CEEs. They are compiling a list of challenges which become the central research agenda for a full-scale, large proposal.

Today, a user of this global infrastructure must trust the infrastructure vendors based on their informal textual contracts. This trust model provides limited legal protection of user interests and has become a key barrier for more services to migrate into the public infrastructure, stymieing innovation and competition.

This project's key novelty is to build highly performant, certified execution environments (CEEs) for large-scale distributed systems. In doing so, the project explores, refines, and discovers design principles for scaling certified trust --- specifically, scaling up to include the entire software stack, and scaling out to include globally distributed resources. The project's main impact is to enable and promote trustworthy, performant, cost-effective uses of the publicglobal infrastructure, empowering applications and services for a global market.

During the Planning stage, the PIs developed a prototype testbed and evaluated the feasibility of building a high-performance trustworthy global-scale mobile network using cloud-scale disaggregated CEEs. They developed a CEE enclave prototype platform leveraging ARM TrustZone; the prototype also supports data-centric data distribution services for enclave communication with our testbed ThinROS library.  The PIs also used simulator models to assess the overheads of the published baseline approaches to sandboxing accelerators; their preliminary results found that prior approaches degraded performance significantly.

The PIs also developed a testbed for the disaggregated architecture and built a prototype OS, called MIND, that can manage resources in a compute-memory disaggregated architecture. They integrated cryptography libraries developed for ThinROS into MIND’s kernel to protect data exchanged via shared memory in a disaggregated enclave. This MIND prototype provides a cache-coherent view of data in the enclave, leveraging a realization of the MSI cache coherence protocol using programmable network switches and RDMA communications for performance and scalability.

In tandem, the PIs began to explore questions pertaining to the integration of untrusted accelerators into a trusted host. As part of this, the PIs used cycle accurate simulation to determine the overheads of modern IOMMUs and memory translation hardware, more broadly.

Finally, the PIs developed a cloud-scale solution for oblivious data accesses, called Shortstack, that enables scalable and fault-tolerant protection against access pattern attacks. Shortstack augments the confidentiality guarantees of our CEE to include provable security against both data and access pattern leakage, while only incurring a small constant factor storage and bandwidth overhead.

Additional highlights include (1) developing a new compositional theory of linearizability which can be used to specify and compose multiple concurrent CEE enclaves to build distributed enclaves, and (2) extending the real-time CertiKOS kernel to support EDF-based partion-based enclave schedulers with temporal and spatial isolation guarantee.

The project also helped prepare the next generations of engineers to apply these ideas through new courses on operating systems, computer networks, and software and hardware interface. The team has also actively educated students on these topics in all parts of the STEM pipeline, ranging from middle- and high school, undergraduate studies to graduate school via engagement with Yale's Pathways to Science program.

abstractText:
The international Physics of Living Systems (iPoLS) graduate research network (GRN) connects graduate students across the globe who are using methods and concepts of physical systems to unravel the mysteries of living dynamics. This inherently interdisciplinary field has undergone a tremendous growth over the past decade, partly as a result of community efforts such as the iPoLS graduate research network. This network enables the creation of coherent training programs, forums for peer-to-peer learning and information transfer, and provides support for efforts to grow the faculty and student numbers in this field at US universities. The current project will continue building the network in the US, and one of the major goals continues to be fostering communication and cooperation across national boundaries. 

The PIs plan to use network resources to share best practices related both to education and into the building and support of a diverse community. They will present innovative plans for the recruitment of undergraduate interns from underrepresented groups, based on the successful experience of several of the network nodes. The PIs will collectively explore mechanisms for advocating for the unique capabilities of PoLS research and PoLS researchers to the broader biology and biomedicine communities, including the creation of PoLS-based sessions at major society meetings in cell biology, neuroscience, and fundamental cancer research.  

This project is being jointly supported by the Physics of Living Systems program in the Division of Physics and the Molecular Biophysics Cluster in the Division of Molecular and Cellular Biosciences.

abstractText:
Cells need to move collectively in nearly all biological processes at the tissue scale. One of the most significant challenges to understanding collective cell motion is determining how single-cell motility strategies affect collective cell behavior at the tissue level. For example, do cells actively sense the direction of motion of their neighbors, or do cells primarily rely on cell-cell adhesion and repulsion from their neighbors to move collectively? To understand the mapping from single-cell properties to collective migration, the PI proposes a combined experimental and computational approach to investigate collective cell migration during convergent extension processes in the developing zebrafish spinal column. Using confocal microscopy and genetic variants, the PI will measure how alterations to cell-cell adhesion and planar cell polarity alter the flow of cells in three dimensions. He will then simulate convergent extension processes in the developing zebrafish spinal column using the deformable particle (DP) model in two and three spatial dimensions in realistic boundary conditions that are both deformable and contractile. The DP model also makes it possible to systematically vary the cell shape, cell-cell adhesion, and single-cell motility strategy. The PI will compare the results of the simulations to those obtained from 3D imaging of cell motion and shape of both wildtype and mutant zebrafish embryos. The proposed work will provide two significant advances to our understanding of collective cell motion: (1) how can we map single-cell properties to features of collective cell migration, and (2) what is a sufficient degree of model complexity to capture important features of collective cell migration? Currently, models for collective cell migration do not model true cell deformability and realistic cell motility strategies, but they can qualitatively capture several aspects of collective cell migration. These proposed simulations of deformable particles in both two and three dimensions, along with three-dimensional imaging of live tissue, will allow the team to determine what model ingredients are required to quantitatively describe collective cell migration. This project also includes a number of education and outreach activities that leverage the PIs' involvement in the Integrated Graduate Program in Physical and Engineering Biology. Initiatives will include mentoring high school and undergraduate students in research, developing a course module on computational modeling of cell migration during zebrafish spinal column development, and hosting short courses aimed at improving the presentation of scientific topics to non-scientific audiences by graduate students.

The PI proposes coordinated experimental and computational studies to understand the role of cell shape change, motility strategy, and adhesion on collective cell motion during the convergent extension process in the elongating tail bud of zebrafish embryos. The PI will develop novel deformable particle (DP) model simulations in dynamic, deformable boundaries in both two and three spatial dimensions, which can quantitatively describe cell- and tissue-level deformation of developing zebrafish embryos and predict the effect of changes to single-cell biophysical parameters on collective cell motion. Complementary experiments will be performed on zebrafish embryos with varied cell motility and cell-cell adhesion through mutations to the planar cell polarity pathway and cadherin-mediated adhesion that enable the predictions of the DP model to be tested experimentally.

projectOutComesReport:
This award supported combined experimental and computational studies to understand collective cell motion during development and in confluent epithelial cell monolayers. In the first project, we focused on the regulation of the mechanical properties of tissues during spinal column development in vertebrate embryos.  We found that a fluid to solid transition is driven by a combination of increased adhesion between cells, increased adhesion between cells and the extracellular matrix and an intrinsic decline in cell motility. Furthermore, a negative feedback loop within the extracellular matrix limits the degree of tissue solidification during development.

In the second project, we focused on understanding the shape changes that occur in epithelial cells as they move in confluent cell monolayers.  When particles are densely packed together, they typically form solid-like states where the individual particles do not rearrange due to the lack of free volume and fixed, rigid shapes of each particle. In contrast, epithelial cells in confluent monolayers, where there is zero free volume, can move since each cell can dynamically adjust its shape. To understand the connection between changes in cell shape and motion, we carried out cell segmentation on time-lapse images of motile epithelial cells in confluent monolayers. We showed that the distribution of cell shape parameters P(A) is broad and positively skewed, where the cell shape parameter A is defined as the ratio of the squared perimeter of a cell to its area. We developed two contrasting computational models to explain cell shape changes: (1) an active deformable particle model with an elastic shape parameter and (2) an active deformable particle model with an adaptive shape parameter. We find that Model 1 is unable to recapitulate P(A) without inducing biologically unrealistic cell strains. However, Model 2 recreates P(A) over a wide range of parameters, suggesting that cells are not elastic in their shape parameter and that cell shapes arise from motion in confluent monolayers.  The adaptive cell shape parameter can be attributed to the regulation of caveolae or lipid vesicles.

The project also partially supported three Ph.D. students in Physics and Biomedical Engineering at Yale, as well as several high school students and undergraduates.

abstractText:
Metamaterials capable of accessing multiple properties will lead to systems possessing a wide range of functions. Such multifunctional metamaterials will increase the autonomy, efficiency, and lifespan of systems and structures by dynamically adapting to task demands or changes in the environment. Granular metamaterials are an advantageous platform for such dynamic programmability, as the grain properties can be widely tuned to achieve different responses. Granular metamaterial response is dependent on many variables, including the grain arrangement, grain mass, modulus, and shape, friction or other interactions between grains, as well as whether the walls of the container are held fixed or can move in response to forces from the grains. With such a vast number of possible combinations of micro-structural variables, the task of designing the complex relationship between micro-structure and bulk properties is daunting. This Designing Materials to Revolutionize and Engineer our Future (DMREF) research applies evolutionary algorithms to efficiently search the immense parameter space of granular metamaterial designs for specific material properties, as well as identifying how a design can be perturbed to actively transition from one set of desired bulk properties to another. The project will establish a new artificial intelligence-driven approach to the design and optimization of granular metamaterials with adaptable properties. These materials will aid US productivity and prosperity by providing additional means to find and use materials impacting robotics and other technical areas.

Future granular metamaterials will exhibit increased dynamic plasticity, enabling responses to different environmental inputs or task demands by reconfiguring their physical structure. This project addresses two issues: (1) How can granular assemblies with specific desired material properties be automatically designed? (i.e., What should the grains' arrangement, moduli, shapes, masses, friction coefficients, and other grain-scale properties be to yield a given bulk material property?); and (2) How can a series of granular assemblies that allow continuous, time-ordered changes in material properties be automatically designed? (i.e., Which set of grain-scale variables should change and by how much? If multiple solutions are found, which ones can be realized in experiments most easily?) To address these issues, a closed-loop procedure will be developed and implemented wherein physics-based discrete element method (DEM) simulations, evolution-based optimization, and physical realizations are combined to produce granular metamaterials with desired, optimal, and adaptable material properties. New knowledge and tools that will be generated by this project include: (i) alternative evolutionary algorithms for designing granular metamaterials capable of changing their own configuration and properties; (ii) physics-based DEM simulations that can predict the properties of granular materials with active grains; and (iii) New synthesis strategies for multifunctional grains and grain assemblies.

abstractText:
This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2). 

Some efforts to manage natural resources have relied on family planning initiatives designed to address broader demographic concerns about population rise. This doctoral dissertation project examines how an understanding of overpopulation connects to efforts to slow fertility rates in vulnerable ecosystems, and what relationship the resulting family planning initiatives have with reproductive behavior. This research project asks how environmental scientists and organizations understand and communicate the relationship between reproduction and conservation. In addition to providing funding for the training of a graduate student in anthropology in the methods of empirical, findings will be disseminated to stakeholder organizations that shape the design and implementation of conservation programs. This project also broadens the participation of groups underrepresented in science.

This doctoral dissertation research project explores the relationship between family planning and environmental conservation policies aimed at addressing population concerns. Through an ethnographic study of demographers, marine scientists, family planning practitioners, and women participating in family planning, the project examines the processes underlying the production of population data, and the relationship these dynamics have to women’s own experiences and understandings of reproductive freedom. Ultimately, this study contributes to new understandings of the ways in which demography and reproductive policy shape women’s reproductive lives. The methods include participant observation, semi-structured interviews and life history interviews with demographic scientists, community-based family planning practitioners, and women of reproductive age, as well as archival data analysis and supply chain mapping. The project contributes to a growing scholarship on the environmental dimensions of reproduction, and advances scholarship in political ecology and science studies more broadly.

projectOutComesReport:
This award was originally intended to fund doctoral dissertation research on family planning and marine conservation in coastal Madagascar. The project was based on three years of Masters-level and preliminary doctoral research in the island’s northwest mangrove communities. However, shortly after the funding of this project, the Covid-19 pandemic halted all international research projects. The Malagasy state restricted access to Madagascar, impeding international travel for research. As a result, the co-PI (M.L.) was unable to access her field site. The project’s intended location was in a rural, forest-dependent community, where residents have limited phone and internet access. These conditions made it nearly impossible to conduct research interviews remotely.

In the face of these serious obstacles to this research project, the co-PI made the difficult decision to shift her project field site to an accessible location within the United States. The project remained focused on the social dimensions of reproductive medicine. However, rather than family planning, the project would now center the practices and experiences of infertility within the U.S.

After spending considerable time sourcing field sites, establishing research relationships, obtaining new IRB approval, and completing HIPPA training, fieldwork began at the outset of 2022. The project would now take place in three in vitro fertilization (IVF) clinics in the northeast United States. The exact names and locations of these clinics remain anonymous to protect the privacy of research participants. While set in a different location and among new actors, the project’s methods remained fundamentally unchanged. The co-PI conducted daily participant observation in a variety of clinical settings, interacting with physicians, nurses, embryologists, and IVF patients. She observed and learned the processes of IVF care, including patient consultations, exams, and procedures. She also spent considerable time alongside clinic embryologists to learn the practices of embryo culture.

The project’s questions were heavily influenced by the June 2022 Supreme Court decision in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, as practitioners and patients in the sphere of IVF adapted to a new political and juridical landscape. As gestating and IVF embryos became the focus of much national attention, I examined how IVF’s varied stakeholders conceptualized the embryos they facilitated, cultured, and handled (in the case of IVF professionals) or intended to parent (in the case of IVF patients). Alongside 15 months of participant observation, I also conducted 30 conversational interviews with clinicians, embryologists, and patients. Data revealed that embryos take on a variety of meanings in the context of IVF, and that these meanings often co-occur. Moreover, owing to their interactions with patients, clinicians play a large role in fostering patients’ (and thus, the public’s) understandings of embryos. Clinicians’ use of language, and understandings of embryos, become politicized when they and their patients take those understandings outside clinic walls.

In Fall 2023, findings were published in the medical anthropology website Somatosphere. This article allowed participants to learn about and engage in the project’s initial conclusions. Following the completion of fieldwork in spring 2024, project findings were presented to clinicians at participating IVF clinics. Over two clinical presentations, participants discussed project findings and the implications for their own practices. Results were presented to academic audiences in conferences including the Association of American Anthropologists annual meeting, and the Society for the Social Studies of Science annual meeting. I also wrote up the project’s findings in a book-length dissertation, which I successfully defended in May 2024. In 2025, results will be further discussed in forthcoming articles in Medical Anthropology Quarterly and Fertility and Sterility, two journals with diverse audiences. Supplementary articles are planned for journals in anthropology and bioethics, culminating in the publication of this project in book form.

abstractText:
This award is funded in whole or in part under the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 (Public Law 117-2).

This project explores the role of material objects in supporting social networks. Archaeological ceramics are uniquely positioned to offer insight on ancient peoples, reflecting both intentional and unintentional aesthetic, technical, and social choices. Building on a long-standing anthropological focus on prestige goods and exchange networks, a distinctive style of ceramic will be investigated. Integrating archaeological, art historical, and compositional data on this little understood social valuable, analysis of the production of these vessels and their movement through the landscape will demonstrate how material objects play a crucial role in the development of social relationships. In addition to contributing to gaps in existing compositional databases and assisting in the evaluation of methods for the chemical characterization of archaeological ceramics, the project will also provide students with the opportunity to gain laboratory skills related to archaeological science. 

Emphasizing the material basis for social networks, this project evaluates hypotheses of open and restricted access to a technically complex ceramic decorative style. Was this style available to the general population or restricted to elite communities? Which potting communities had access to the technical artistry required to produce these vessels, and did every community produce them using the same technique? Who exchanged ceramics with whom? Answering these questions furthers understandings of how social networks are supported and maintained by economically and symbolically significant social valuables. This project will use bulk compositional data acquired using instrumental neutron activation analysis, surface compositional data acquired using portable x-ray fluorescence, microscopic analysis of surface treatment, and data on style and form to trace interaction between archaeological sites. Examining the production of and access to these socially significant objects will illuminate systems of pottery production on a regional scale and the ways in which human relationships are negotiated and constructed through material means on a broader level.

projectOutComesReport:
Usulutan pottery was made by ancient people living in El Salvador and Guatemala between the years 700 BCE and 400 CE. The pottery is decorated using a special process, resulting in a bichromatic pattern of orange and yellow. Vessels with this decoration are well known from elaborate burials, but also appear in feasting contexts. Despite the abundance of Usulutan pottery in the Southern Maya Region, there has never been a systematic study. This grant supported an investigation of Usulutan pottery from an archaeometric perspective, thinking about production, exchange, and access. The goal was to better understand the role of Usulutan in supporting social structures.

Compositional analyses of archaeological ceramics can provide valuable archaeometric data related to the production, decoration, and exchange of pottery. This project embraced a portable methodology based around sampling previously excavated archaeological ceramics in museum collections. Eleven museums in the United States and Guatemala supplied ceramics for both destructive and nondestructive materials analysis. Archaeological sites represented in the ceramic dataset include Chalchuapa, Cotzumalhuapa, Isla El Espiritu Santo, Kaminaljuyú, Marinalá, Salinas La Blanca, Sin Cabezas, Tiquisate, and unprovenanced. Compositional data on the paste of over two hundred Usulután vessels was acquired using both portable X-ray fluorescence (pXRF) and instrumental neutron activation analysis (INAA). A DinoLite digital microscope was used to examine and record the vessel paste.

The 217 ceramic samples were classified into compositional groups A-H based on multivariate statistics. These groups were then compared to reference data on clays and ceramics from the area to determine likely source locations. Group A is found exclusively at the large regional centers of Kaminaljuyu and Chalchuapa. This group includes more complex vessel shapes and designs than other groups. Group A shows similarities to clays from the highlands, suggesting production around Kaminaljuyu. Group B is found mostly at Kaminaljuyu, but also smaller sites in the piedmont and is likely from the highlands. Group C is found predominantly at Sin Cabezas, with a few sherds at other sites. It shows strong compositional similarities to references from this Escuintla. Group D is found at Chalchuapa, but also at large and medium sites in Guatemala. Group D is most similar to reference material from Western El Salvador. Group E includes only samples from Cotzumalhuapa, which were likely made there. Group F is a mixed group not dominated by any one site, perhaps suggesting it originates from further away. Group G is found at Cotzumalhuapa and Isla El Espiritu Santo, and shows similarities to Escuintla clays. Group H includes only ceramics from Marinala and was likely produced near the site in Escuintla.

The largest cities, Kaminaljuyu and Chalchuapa, reveal different patterns. At Chalchuapa, 84% of the Usulután was locally produced. Only 15 % of the Usulután at Chalchuapa was from non-local sources, with a small amount from the Group A source associated with Kaminaljuyu. This is a stark contrast to Kaminaljuyú, where roughly 58% of the Usulután is local. The rest of the Usulutan at Kaminaljuyu is from non-local sources, mostly from Chalchuapa. While local production is common at Kaminaljuyú, there is a significant quantity of imported pottery. It is notable that the relationship between these sites is not reciprocal – Kaminaljuyu imports much more Usulutan than Chalchuapa. Looking at medium-sized sites in the piedmont shows further diversity. Cotzumalhuapa has the most compositional groups at any one site. 48% of the Usulután at Cotzumalhuapa is local, produced using two clay sources. The non-local pottery at Cotzumalhuapa makes up 50.23% of the Usulután at the site, and links the site to Sin Cabezas, the Guatemalan highlands, and Western El Salvador. Marinalá and Sin Cabezas follow an alternative pattern. People at Marinalá received 77.77% of their Usulután from the local Group H, which exclusively supplied the people in this city. At Sin Cabezas, 84.37% of the pottery is from local Group C. A small quantity of highland pottery is found at each site, but not in the quantities as at Cotzumalhuapa. Sin Cabezas also has a small amount of pottery from Chalchuapa’s Group D. Turning our attention to the smaller sites of Salinas La Blanca and Isla El Espiritu Santo reveals that neither small sites was producing their own Usulután pottery.

The compositional data indicates that Usulutan was a multifaceted tool for social interaction. People most likely shared meals using these patterned vessels during a myriad of social events. Group A vessels are found only at large centers and show a higher level of technical complexity than other groups, suggesting that these vessels were restricted to social interactions between elites. In contrast, Group H vessels are found only at the minor site of Marinala, indicating production focused on social events for people living in the city. Overall, Usulután pottery was an important component of the interaction between city-states, providing an avenue for the reinforcing of social bonds.

abstractText:
NON-TECHNICAL SUMMARY

When a liquid is cooled to become a solid, like water solidifying into ice when cooled in a freezer, the atoms could form a crystalline solid, where the atoms are arranged periodically, or a glass, where the atoms are arranged randomly. Metal alloys can form metallic glasses when cooled rapidly. Metallic glasses have properties that suggest improvements in applications such as casings for electronics, batteries, and hydrogen, for medical devices and implants, and applications in space for robotics gears and satellite tanks. Whether the liquid becomes crystalline or a glass depends on the cooling rate; the faster the liquid is cooled, the more likely it will form a glass.  The slowest cooling rate that still allows for glass formation is the critical cooling rate, which is a key characteristic of any material. Determining critical cooling rates and hence, quantifying the glass forming ability (GFA), has been a very difficult and elaborate task in the past. Recent work by the PI revealed that the GFA can be determined from the structure of the glassy solid through x-ray diffraction measurements that gives information on the arrangement of the atoms.  Correlating these x-ray diffraction measurements to the GFA provides a cutting-edge tool that will advance the science of glasses and liquids significantly.  Thereby, this research has the potential to develop new metallic glasses faster to be used in a wide range of applications and impact US manufacturing. The PI will also train the next generation of scientist through an open, interactive approach in the spirit of the Materials Genome Initiative (MGI) by broadly sharing all experimental data with the scientific community and through outreach programs where high-school students learn and teach about cutting edge materials science research by making YouTube videos. 

TECHNICAL SUMMARY

Vitrification, the formation of a glass upon solidification of a liquid metal, which is quantified in the critical cooling rate and referred to as the glass forming ability, GFA, is a key characteristic of paramount importance for the physics, formation and processing of glasses. However, quantifying glass forming ability has been experimentally elaborate and its complexity has prevented use of computational methods. These challenges have impeded progress in metallic glass science, discovery and technology which takes place in a vast potential compositional space.  Preliminary results by the PI suggest that this grant can overcome previous limitations of identifying GFA of alloys. The PI provides evidence that the GFA is reflected in the structure the glass assumes and this structure can be readily measured with standard x-ray diffraction measurements. The alloy’s atomic structure is quantified in the full-width-half-max of the first diffraction peak in the XRD spectrum, Dq, and the PI’s preliminary results reveals a direct correlation between Dq and GFA; Best glass formers exhibit the most disordered amorphous structure, reflected in their highest Dq in their as-sputtered state which is furthest away from equilibrium. The Dq-GFA relationship suggested that current models to describe the atomic structure of metallic glasses are limited to the ideal glass state but do not describe the, vastly larger in number, real glasses that occupy the higher potential energy states in the potential energy landscape. To describe such real glasses, contributions of entropy, and possibly kinetics have to be considered as well.  Separately, by exploring the Dq-GFA relationship over large compositional spaces and temperatures or cooling rates, will provide insight into formation motifs of metallic glasses.

projectOutComesReport:
To discover new alloys, commonly sputtering of the various alloy elements to generate thin film libraries of alloys is used. Such combinatorial sputtering is experimentally very effective.

However, there are points of concern where the thin film may no longer represent the bulk alloy of interest. Such concerns originate from the i.) small dimension of the thin film, < 1micron, which is smaller than the longest length scale in an alloy’s microstructure ii.) fast cooling rates that result in a solidification product which is typically far away from equilibrium and hence, away from the bulk alloy. The second point can be readily address by annealing and or controlled cooling the film after sputtering. However, the small dimension of the thin films are a fundamental limitation to the usefulness of the thin film representing the bulk sample. It has been shown that phase structure and fraction is the same in thin film and bulk (cooled under same rates). However, phase morphology is different where at a minimum, grains are limited in growing tall and are forced into other shapes that are confined by the thin film geometry.

One aspect that has received relatively little attention about the potential difference between sputtering and bulk solidification has been the nature of the crystallization process. To date, there is no quantitative analysis that allows to conclude about the solidification process during magnetron sputtering. In equilibrium an alloy can sample all possible combinations of phases at all combinations where their sum leads to the composition of the nominal composition. Such solidification or crystallization is referred to as polymorphic crystallization.  At some very high cooling rate, no long-distance diffusion is possible due to the reduced available timescale and only phases (crystalline and amorphous) can form that are at the same composition than the nominal composition. Such solidification is referred to as non-polymorphic crystallization. Obviously, complexity, mechanism, thermodynamic, and kinetic of these two processes, polymorphic crystallization vs. non-polymorphic crystallization are very different. During this funding period we researched what crystallization mechanism is present during magnetron sputtering. This is very important to know as it will tell us if thin film samples made through magnetron sputtering can be used to represent the bulk alloy.

We examined our sputtering data on almost 60 alloys. We found that when two phases form during sputtering these phases exhibit some difference in composition. Hence, magnetron sputtering can still lead to polymorphic solidification in alloys. This finding has important ramification for the use of sputtering and combinatorial sputtering in alloy development where the developed alloy is intended to be used in a bulk form. Magnetron sputtering represent both aspects of crystallization, the formation of multiple phases and the compositional changes within multiple phases. Thereby, magnetron sputtering can be used to provide information about the solidification of alloys in a more general form besides the polymorphic limit.

abstractText:
The number and severity of abnormal weather events, such as storms and droughts, have increased in recent decades all over the world. In the tropical forests of South America, two large drought events occurred in 2005 and 2010, and more will likely happen in the future. Although most tropical forests have a regular and predictable dry season that lasts several months, those that lie in the northwestern corner of the Amazon region do not. Here, high rainfall occurs in every month of the year, and researchers think that these forests may be hit particularly hard by lower rainfall. No one knows if these trees have had any previous experience of drought conditions. If they do grow poorly or die when there is no rain, then the kinds of trees that make up these forests may be quite different in future, leading to changes in how the forest works, as well as in the availability of food for animals and resources for people. This International Research Experiences for Students (IRES) project will carry out experiments to look at how tree seedlings of this area respond to drought, and how drought affects the other animals that interact with trees. The award addresses a critical scientific challenge while building capacity and experience in field and lab techniques among U.S. graduate and undergraduate students. To this end, we will mentor six U.S. students every year during the spring semester before, and fall semester after, they embark on an overseas research experience in Ecuador, working with long-term collaborators of PIs Queenborough and Metz at Pontificia Universidad Catolica del Ecuador, as well as with Ecuadorian students. Masters’ and undergraduate students from Yale University will be paired with undergraduates from Lewis & Clark College, a primarily undergraduate institution, to develop and conduct ecological research in a remote field station in the Amazon rain forest: Yasuni National Park.

This project will address a key knowledge gap in forest ecology and climate change science: how do aseasonal ever-wet tropical forests respond to drought and natural enemies? The answer has clear implications for theoretical ecology (how infrequent disturbance, i.e., drought, affects the dynamics and composition of diverse ecological communities), climate change ecology (how forest structure, composition and distribution will likely change in the future), and policy (whether tropical forests remain a net carbon sink, or switch to a net carbon source thereby accelerating climate change). Tropical aseasonal ever-wet rain forests are characterized by high rainfall and no dry season, as well as high biological diversity and globally significant carbon stocks. However, anthropogenic climate change is predicted to lead to increases in the frequency and severity of droughts in South America. Drought is expected to act synergistically with other abiotic and biotic factors such as the pests and pathogens that drive the negative density-dependence that helps maintain the high diversity found in the tropics. Recent work has focused on the impacts of drought on tropical seasonal forests, yet virtually nothing is known about how pest and pathogen pressure varies with water availability in the aseasonal ever-wet tropics nor how increasing drying may change the structure and function of these forests. This project, therefore, will investigate the interaction between climate and natural enemies on the performance of trees in a hyper-diverse, aseasonal tropical rain forest in the northwestern Amazon. Specifically, the research team will use experiments to test the effect of variation in water availability on pest and pathogen attack on young seedlings and how these effects will likely alter the strength and direction of negative density dependence; this information will transform current theoretical understanding of how these two factors affect tree performance, diversity, and distributions. Results will also provide key information on how these economically and ecologically valuable, yet largely unknown, forests will change in a future of increasing drought. The prime goal of this project is to build capacity and experience in field and lab techniques among U.S. graduate and undergraduate students. To this end, the PIs will mentor six U.S. students every year during the spring semester before, and fall semester after, they embark on an overseas research experience in Ecuador, working with long-term collaborators of PIs Queenborough and Metz at Pontificia Universidad Catolica del Ecuador, as well as with Ecuadorian students. Masters and undergraduate students from Yale University will be paired with undergraduates from Lewis & Clark College, a primarily undergraduate institution, to develop and conduct ecological research in a remote field station in the Amazon rain forest: Yasuni National Park. Yasuni National Park and the associated Forest Dynamics Plot are unique scientific resources. Exposing U.S. students to the incredible richness of the most diverse forest in the world is an inspiring and humbling experience. Students will be involved in meaningful research that is directly contributing to a broad understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that structure ecosystems and communities. Ensuring that students understand how such science is conducted and how they can contribute is essential for how future generations decide to manage the world they inherit.

projectOutComesReport:
The prime goal of this project was to build capacity and experience in ecological field and lab techniques among US graduate and undergraduate students. An annual cohort of students participated in an immersive and closely mentored research experience to study tropical forest diversity and dynamics in Yasuní National Park in Amazonian Ecuador, one of the most biodiverse forests on earth. Exposing students to the incredible richness found in the forests of western Amazonia is an inspiring and humbling experience. We involved them in research that is contributing directly to our understanding of the fundamental mechanisms that structure ecosystems and communities.



To this end, we mentored cohorts of US students every year during the spring semester before, and fall semester after, they embarked on an overseas summer research experience in Ecuador, working with long-term Ecuadorian collaborators. Masters and undergraduate students from Yale University were paired with undergraduates from Lewis & Clark College, a primarily undergraduate institution, to develop and conduct ecological research in a remote field station in the Amazon rain forest. The students gained experience in every stage of scientific research: exploring the tropical ecology scientific literature to contextualize and develop research questions, living and working in a remote and arduous field environment, collecting data, learning code and analytical techniques, writing and publication, as well as the process of peer review and revision. This process was facilitated by intensive mentoring from US and Ecuadorian senior researchers. In addition, participants developed many transferable skills such as coding, data analysis, communicating research, and logical writing that will support their future scientific research careers and contribute to the US scientific workforce. The program also broadened access to international STEM research for US students and strengthened existing research collaborations between Ecuadorian and US research institutions.



In this hyperdiverse region, the lack of a predictable seasonal drought is a key driver of organismal diversity, structure, and function. We mentored 12 undergraduate and four master’s students over the four years of this project. The individual student projects were based on understanding how organisms interact with their local environment and the other plants and animals within it. Specific projects included leaf morphology, drivers of herbivory, understory terrestrial herbs, and interactions between plants and insects. Student-led research supported by this project has been published in top peer-reviewed journals and presented at local and national meetings of scientists. They are now employed in environmental sectors that include habitat restoration or botanic gardens or enrolled in further education such as a master’s in environmental science or medical school. Pre- and post-experience surveys revealed our alumni increased their confidence in their identity as a scientist and cited the research experience as a strong component of post-education career decisions. Ensuring that students understand how science is conducted and how they can contribute is essential for how future generations decide to manage the world they inherit.
