abstractText:
Microscopic fossil shells can provide records of ocean chemistry in the past. The boron to calcium ratio (B/Ca) and boron isotopic composition (d11B) of such fossils are widely used to record seawater pH and carbon chemistry. These records provide valuable insights into past changes in atmospheric carbon dioxide and the global carbon cycle. Recent experiments show that the addition of sulfate ions increases the amount of B incorporated into carbonate minerals. The proposed study will explore how and why B incorporation is enhanced by sulfate. It also will examine if sulfate influences the d11B of synthetic calcite. And the study will use culture experiments to assess whether the boron chemistry of biogenic calcite is impacted by seawater sulfate. This will be a crucial test of the reliability of d11B and B/Ca fossil records, since seawater sulfate has varied substantially over the last 60 million years. The project also will provide training for graduate and undergraduate students and educational outreach activities to local communities. 

This study integrates inorganic calcite precipitation experiments and foraminiferal culturing to investigate the mechanistic link between B incorporation and sulfate (SO42−) and its relevance to biological systems using benthic foraminifers as the model organism. First, we will comprehensively analyze δ11B, B/Ca and other trace elements (S/Ca and Na/Ca) of synthetic calcite precipitated in solutions added with aqueous B and variable amounts of SO42−. Second, we will grow sub-mm scale calcite crystals in growth solutions added with aqueous B and/or SO42−, and compare the intra-crystal distribution/zonation of B and S using a secondary ion mass spectrometer (SIMS). Finally, we will culture a well-studied species of benthic foraminifera under various seawater SO42− concentrations. If foraminiferal δ11B and B/Ca are indeed sensitive to changes in seawater SO42−, we will provide the equations to account for the SO42− effect.

projectOutComesReport:
The major goal of this project was to test the influence of seawater sulfate on the boron isotopic composition of calcite minerals formed in marine environments, a widely used geochemical proxy for seawater pH that has been used to investigate ocean acidification events in the geologic past. Reconstructing these past acidification events is of crucial importance for understanding modern ocean acidification and the degree to which it may proceed in the future with ongoing anthropogenic CO2 emissions. However, accurate pH reconstruction from boron isotopes requires a careful understanding of past changes in seawater chemistry. Our project explored whether past changes in seawater sulfate concentrations may influence the boron isotopic composition of calcite, using laboratory experiments in which we varied the concentration of sulfate in solution while precipitating calcite minerals. Our results showed that increasing sulfate concentrations decreases calcite precipitation rates, increases boron incorporation into calcite, and drives the boron isotopic composition toward lighter values, which is the opposite of what previous studies predicted. We proposed that sulfate incorporation into calcite distorts the calcite crystal lattice, enhancing incorporation of isotopically light borate ions and driving the overall boron isotopic composition lighter. Given that seawater sulfate concentrations are thought to have been lower in the geologic past, our findings suggest potential error in pH calculations for older calcite samples, and point toward the need for considering sulfate concentrations in future attempts to reconstruct pH from boron isotopes across Earth history.

Beyond its research impacts, this project has supported the training of graduate students in laboratory techniques that are highly transferrable across a wide range of disciplines. As part of this project, collaborators have participated in public outreach events to disseminate knowledge on ocean acidification and its relationship to climate change. More broadly, our work contributes to further refine our ability to characterize past ocean acidification events, which set the baseline for predicting the environmental consequences of ongoing anthropogenic carbon emissions.

abstractText:
Air pollution causes major health problems and is responsible for 8 million deaths annually worldwide. Reactive organic chemicals (ROCs) are the key precursors that make up smog. In the past, research on the emissions of ROCs has focused primarily on combustion sources from cars and trucks. However, non-combustion ROC sources such as roofing and paving materials, building materials, and consumer products and packaging are now understood to play a larger role in air quality. In spite of this recognition, reliable data on the magnitude and chemical makeup of ROC emissions from non-combustion sources is very limited. Such information is critical to understanding their impact on human health and the environment. The goal of this project is to address this need by investigating the emissions of complex mixtures of ROCs from non-combustion sources. The research will be performed using specially designed reaction chambers using cutting-edge analytical techniques and tools. Successful completion of this project will benefit society by increasing our understanding of pollutant emissions that impact both outdoor and indoor air quality. Further benefits to society from this project result from education and training opportunities to graduate students, undergraduate students, and high school interns. The investigator will promote diversity and enhance the involvement of under-represented groups in science and engineering through engagement in Yale's K-12 outreach activities. 

Emissions from non-combustion sources are increasingly understood to play a larger role in air quality. The goal of this project is to address knowledge gaps on emissions of gas-phase reactive organic compounds (ROCs) from emerging non-combustion sources and their subsequent chemical transformations in urban air. To achieve this goal, the PI and collaborators at Aerodyne Research will focus on the characterization of ROCs generated by mixtures of known, understudied, and unknown organic chemicals. The team will carry out experiments in emission and reaction chambers using a suite of state-of-the-art high-resolution mass spectrometry and gas/liquid chromatography. The research will include “bottom-up” emissions experiments to quantify the magnitude and chemical composition of emissions from paving and roofing asphalt materials, two of the most important non-combustion sources of ROCs. A major focus of these experiments will be on poorly constrained emissions pathways and compound classes. In addition, the team will also conduct experiments in an oxidation flow reactor to 1) determine the oxidation products and secondary organic aerosol yields from model and relevant precursor mixtures emitted from non-combustion sources, and 2) identify key single precursors present in these complex mixtures. The PI will pursue active collaboration with emissions inventory and modeling experts at the U.S. EPA and other stakeholders to disseminate information and data resulting from this study. The successful completion of this project has potential for transformative impact in air pollution management through the development of new insight and fundamental knowledge on the emission, fate, and atmospheric chemistry of ROCs emitted from non-combustion sources.

projectOutComesReport:
The overarching goal of this project was to examine non-traditional sources of reactive organic gases, while also training future generations of scientists, engineers, and other STEM professionals. This included volatile, intermediate-volatility, and semi-volatile organic compounds (VOCs, IVOCs, SVOCs), which can impact air quality as either primary pollutants or as precursors to secondary pollution (e.g., particulate matter (PM2.5), tropospheric ozone), with implications spanning from regional/local outdoor areas down to indoor environments. With successful reductions in emissions from motor vehicles over the past 50+ years, the consideration of other non-combustion-related sources has become increasingly important for understanding the chemical composition of the urban atmosphere and urban air quality, including variations across spatial and temporal scales. As such, the project targeted knowledge gaps with intellectual merit in the disciplines of outdoor and indoor air quality, as well as broader impacts through knowledge that can lead to improvements in air quality. This work has examined a range of sources, spanning emissions from materials/products used indoors, to emissions from materials used in the outdoor urban built environment, cooking- and tobacco-related emissions of gases and particles, and also emissions from oil sands operations. In addition to examining the rates and chemical composition of emissions, other foci have been on reservoirs with emissions occurring over both short- and long-term timescales (e.g., off-gassing) and the influence of environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, solar radiation). This research has incorporated the use of laboratory emissions experiments, oxidation flow reactor and chamber experiments to examine chemical oxidation, and outdoor ambient data to investigate chemically-complex emissions from a range of sources as well as their chemical transformations. Powerful chemically-resolved measurement methods were advanced and applied over the course of this research and associated collaborations, including the application of ammonium-adduct chemical ionization mass spectrometry, in collaboration with industry partners, to measure a wide range of oxygenated VOCs emitted from non-traditional sources in urban areas. This project included valuable industry collaborations with Aerodyne Research Inc., as well as engagement with other analytical chemistry companies (e.g., Gerstel) to advance applications through this research.

 

In addition to the broader impacts associated with studies on air quality, the project also achieved broader impacts through its educational and outreach objectives. K-12 outreach activities focused on afterschool and out-of-school science programs. The project contributed substantially to the professional development of graduate students, undergraduate students, and postdocs. This included 6 PhD students, 2 postdocs, and 14 undergraduates mentored across the course of the project, with an emphasis on sustained multi-semester undergraduate involvement to foster career development in STEM areas. To date, the award has contributed to 2 PhD dissertations and 10 published manuscripts, including in high-impact journals (e.g., Science, Environmental Science & Technology, Atmospheric Chemistry & Physics), as well as presentations (e.g., conferences, workshops, seminars) by multiple members of the research team to disseminate results. Results have also been disseminated through collaborations with domestic and international government agencies (i.e., U.S. EPA, NOAA, Environment and Climate Change Canada). The project provided exposure for junior researchers to state-of-the-science research topics and/or methods with opportunities to learn how to operate or work with data from advanced analytical chemistry instrumentation employing mass spectrometry, gas/liquid chromatography, or other methods/approaches applied in the group. This provided training for students and postdocs on advanced methods and instrumentation, as well as technical proficiency, exposure, and professional connections to analytical chemistry companies. The undergraduate/graduate students and postdocs associated with this project are pursuing a range of careers with positions as PhD students, governmental scientists, academic positions, and also in industry.

abstractText:
The aim of this project is to conduct new experimental and theoretical studies on the properties of mineral in the deep interior of Earth that will help us to understand the nature of global water circulation in Earth’s mantle. Not only on the surface, water (hydrogen) is present inside of Earth and slowly circulates. This global water circulation creates and maintains oceans on Earth. Based on a number of studies during the last a few decades, there is a clear idea about the water circulation in the shallow part of Earth’s interior. However, the nature of water circulation in the largest part of the mantle, the lower mantle, remains poorly constrained. A key in the global water circulation is the role of melting. Melting removes water from minerals to melt, and melt migrates a long distance to cause large-scale water transport. However, the nature of global water circulation in the deep mantle is very poorly understood mainly because our understanding of water in the minerals in the deep mantle is limited.  The PI team will bring together a suite of theoretical and experimental methods to address these questions, and will train both graduate and undergraduate students at three institutions on a cross-cutting research project.  The PIs will also engage in public outreach events.

In this new project, the water solubility in bridgmanite (dominant lower mantle mineral) will be determined under the shallow lower mantle conditions from ~660 km to ~1000 km depth, and also the role of water (hydrogen) on electrical conductivity in bridgmanite will be investigated. Experimental studies will be made on clean single crystals of bridgmanite and the hydrogen content and solubility mechanisms will be studied using FTIR and SIMS. Electrical conductivity will be measured on these samples for different orientations using the AC impedance spectroscopy. First-principle computational studies will also be made on hydrogen solubility and mobility in bridgmanite to help interpreting the experimental results. These results will help us to develop a model of global water circulation and to test models against geophysical estimates of water distribution.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of this project is to provide new experimental data on hydrogen dissolution in ilower mantle minerals and new theoretical calculations on melt properties under the deep mantle conditions to help understand the nature of global water circulation.

It is well recognized that both the atmosphere and the oceans on Earth have been there as a result of global water circulation.This implies that both atmosphere and the oceans aren on Earth's suface as a result of the dynamic balance not by static equilibrium: rate of addition of atmosphere and the oceans (degassing) and the rate of removal of those volatile materials back into Earth's interior (regassing) seem to make a balance. However, when dynamic balance controls the mass of atmosphere and the oceans, consequence of these competing processes needs to be understand in detail. Ocean mass (and atomsphetre mass) would be nearly constant only when these two competing processes result in the negative feedback.

Geological observations provide a data set indicating that the sea level as been nearly constant at least for the last ~600 Myrs. However, the sea levels also show large fluctions (a few 100s m) with short timescales (100-200 Myrs). Sea level has been going down for the last ~200 Myrs, and if this trend contiues, oceans will be dried up in less than 1 billion years. This implies that theer are some procsses that stabilize. 

In the past, when scientists investigate these processes, they considered degassing (loss of gass (water etc.) from the mantle to the surface) at mid-oceani ridges and reagssing (return of gasses back to hte mantle) at subduction zones. However, a simple calculation shows that the degassing rate at mid-ocean ridges is too small to explain the observed fast recovery of the sea level. This is large due to the fact that mid-ocean ridge basalts contain only a small amount fo water (~0.1 wt%) and its upwelling rate is slow.

In the meantime, high-pressure studies showed that minerals in the mantle transition zone (the MTZ) have much higher water solubility than minerals above or below the MTZ. Also based on geophysically inferred electrical conductivity distribution, it was shown that the MTZ has a higher water content than regions both below and above. These observations predict that partial melting likely occurs both above and below the MTZ. Melts formed in regions should have much higher water content (to ~10 wt%), and consequently, melting and melt transport actoss the MTZ would play a key role in the global water circulation.

The key issues that we have focused our attebation in this project include (i) detailed charactyerization of hydrogendissolution in bridgmanite (a key mineral in the lower mantle), (ii) partial melting experiments to explore the consequence of partial melting under these conditions, (iii) computational studies on the melt structure and density under the lower mantle conditions, and (iv) the synthesis of these results.

abstractText:
Mammalian hibernation is fascinating. During a short period of time, hibernating animals undergo dramatic adaptive changes, including reduction in heart and respiration rate and decrease of core body temperature from 37°C (98.6°F) to 4°C (39°F), yet they do not experience cold-induced pain, and their organs continue to function despite being cold, non-functional, and deprived of oxygen for eight months out of the year. Moreover, during hibernation, animals do not drink; therefore, hibernators must rely solely on the management and utilization of internal resources for long-term survival. This project seeks to understand the molecular mechanisms that allows hibernators to survive for months without water, using a range of cutting-edge tools and approaches not been previously used for hibernation research, such as optogenetics and fiber photometry. The outcomes of this study will have broad scientific implications, including a better understanding of general mechanisms that regulate internal water and ionic balance common to all mammals. This project also involves educational and outreach efforts in the context of an extracurricular educational program (Sensory Physiology Club) that promotes scientific knowledge in human and animal physiology among school students from middle- and high schools from Connecticut, New York, and Massachusetts. The efforts are designed to spark interest in biological science through lectures and interactive experimental activities that go beyond the science curricula of most schools.

The main scientific goal of this study is to broaden our limited understanding of fluid homeostasis in mammals at the cellular, molecular, and circuit levels by studying ground squirrels during hibernation. This project tests the hypothesis that ground squirrels endure long-term water deprivation in part by modifying the hypothalamic axis, which controls thirst and mediates the release of antidiuretic hormones. Specific aims of this proposal include investigation of the neuronal mechanisms that support the release of vasopressin and oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, and suppress water-seeking behavior during hibernation. This project combines cellular, molecular, and organismal levels of research and uses tools and approaches from a spectrum of disciplines: state-specific biochemical analysis of neuropeptides and hormones, quantitative analysis of hormonal production, differential transcriptomics, electron microscopic and morphometric analyses of hormonal release, and behavioral analyses of drinking behavior. A major innovative aspect of this project is the use of optogenetics, fiber photometry, and electrophysiological tools, which have not been used previously with hibernating animals. The outcomes of this study will delineate general principles of fluid-ionic balance fine-tuning, suggest a strategy to sustain life when water is unavailable, and predict whether hibernation can be induced in other mammals.

projectOutComesReport:
Hibernators stably exist in two distinct neurophysiological states, and thus provide a unique opportunity to dissect general pathways that control fluid homeostasis in mammals from a unique comparative perspective. Squirrels hibernate for 6-8 months of the year without access to water. Even when water is provided, squirrels during hibernation refuse to drink, indicating that drinking behavior is inhibited. That these squirrels can endure such a long period of time without drinking represents a remarkable physiological phenomenon, but the neurophysiological and molecular mechanisms are unknown despite more than one century’s worth of research.

Here we addressed two major questions of high biological and clinical significance. First, how hibernators maintain fluid ionic balance (stay hydrated) despite water deprivation for several months. Second, what is the neurophysiological mechanism of thirst inhibition.

There are several major scientific outcomes of this work. We demonstrated that hypothalamic-pituitary axis fully engaged at the body temperature as low as 10°C that is prohibitive for these processes in non-hibernating species. We also performed in vivo fiber photometry across physiological states and during torpor-arousal cycle and found brain osmosensitive neurons (neurons that detect salt concentration in the blood) can be activated in a dose-dependent manner even before squirrels reach 5°C during early arousal from torpor. We also revealed that long-term survival without water can occurs despite hormonal and behavioral signs of a dramatic fluid deficit and originates from hypoactivity of thirst neurons in circumventricular organs which control of fluid homeostasis. To our knowledge, this is the first study that demonstrates functional decoupling between neuroendocrine pathways that control fluid-ionic balance and behavioral mechanisms that enable water seeking.

Our findings reveal a multi-tiered physiological mechanism of long-term survival without water. This work will facilitate the development of strategies to induce hibernation in humans, a necessary prerequisite for long-term space travel.  We also believe our study has a very broad appeal, beyond the scientific community, since most everyone knows that hibernators have the fascinating ability to withstand very low environmental temperatures without food and water for a long time.

Broader impact of this project was achieved through Sensory Physiology Club, an extracurricular outreach program aimed at sparking interest in biology through lectures and interactive lab activities, which go beyond standard school curricula. Our lectures are also made available via the Internet. The Club facilitates career development of our trainees, postdocs, graduate and undergraduate students as educator-researchers and promotes STEM education among school students of ethnic and economic backgrounds traditionally underrepresented in science. All our teaching activities are free of charge. In addition to individual lectures and laboratory activities, we developed an extended course of five sessions, 1.5 hours each, which we delivered over five days during summer to the same group of school students (usually 15-20 high school students). Overall, we have taught 1100 school students from Connecticut. We are constantly updating lecture material based on the recently published articles, as well as adjusting and improving our lectures and lab activities based on the students’ evaluations.

abstractText:
Agricultural irrigation is the largest user of water in the United States, accounting for approximately 80 percent of the Nation’s clean water consumption. Seawater desalination is a drought-proof technology that can address growing demands for water in agriculture and other uses. At present, seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) is the best available commercially available desalination technology. However, the desalinated seawater cannot be used directly in irrigation due to the limited ability to remove boron. This results from limitations on the boron retention capability of commercial SWRO membranes. Boron adversely impacts plant growth and damages apple, citrus, grapes, and other crops when water containing more than 0.3 mg/L of boron is used in irrigation. Thus, commercial SWRO plants must use an additional purification step to reduce boron concentration to acceptable concentrations. This greatly increases the energy consumption and costs of using desalinated water for agriculture. The proposed research will address the inefficiencies associated with boron removal through the development of a novel selective separation technology based on electrosorption. This new technology will be chemical-free, energy efficient, and capable of recovering a high purity boron stream for beneficial uses. Successful completion of this project will advance the development of the next generation of sustainable SWRO plants, with great potential benefit to society. The project will fruther benefit society by providing research training to graduate and undergraduate students at Yale University. Also, the investigator will promote diversity and enhance the involvement of under-represented groups in science and engineering through engagement in Yale's K-12 outreach activities. 

A critical and unresolved challenge in SWRO desalination is to produce a permeate water stream suitable for irrigation without additional and costly purification to remove plant-toxic elements such as boron. The overall goal of this project is to develop an innovative flow-through electrosorption process for boron removal and recovery in seawater desalination. To achieve this goal, the PI proposes to carry out an integrated experimental and modeling project structured around the following tasks: 1) fabrication of an ultra-selective positive electrode (anode) using boron-chelating resins as building blocks; 2) performance testing of the fabricated electrodes for selective boron removal and recovery; 3) elucidation of the mechanisms underlying selective boron electrosorption; 4) assessment of the impact of electrochemical reactions on the long-term stability and boron selectivity of the electrodes; and 5) evaluation and modeling of the energy consumption and boron selectivity of the combined SWRO-electrosorption process. The proposed work would be the first to study boron-selective removal and recovery from seawater using a chemical-free method. The successful completion of this research has potential to transform desalination through the development of a more energy efficient and sustainable boron removal and recovery process from SWRO plants.

projectOutComesReport:
Boron is a widespread element in seawater, with concentrations ranging from 4-6 ppm. It has also been widely detected in groundwater. Plants are sensitive to boron levels, with both deficiency and excess being harmful. Since irrigation accounts for 70% of global water use, effective boron removal in seawater desalination is crucial. Although boron is a troubling contaminant, it is also a highly versatile and valuable resource, second only to carbon in terms of applications. As both seawater desalination and boron use continue to grow, the need for efficient boron removal and recovery technologies becomes increasingly important.

Despite constituting only 0.01% of the total dissolved solids in seawater, boron removal consumes a disproportionately large amount of energy and chemicals in seawater desalination. To convert boric acid into the more readily removable anion (i.e., borate), the pH of the water must be raised above its pKa of 9.2, typically by adding caustic solutions. However, this high pH environment leads to inorganic scaling on RO membranes due to the natural hardness of seawater. To protect the integrity of RO membranes, boron removal is typically performed in a separate step after nearly all other ions have been removed in a conventional seawater reverse osmosis (SWRO) desalination scheme. Multi-pass RO, though inefficient in terms of energy and chemical use, is still employed in even the largest state-of-the-art desalination facilities, such as the Sorek and Ashkelon plants at Israel, which together produce over 200 million gallons of desalinated water per day. Another widely used boron removal method is boron-selective adsorption. Another widely used method for boron removal is boron-selective adsorption. However, the major shortcomings of both techniques—their high chemical and energy requirements—underscore the urgent need for more sustainable and efficient boron removal technologies.

This project develops an innovative electrosorption process for boron removal and recovery in seawater desalination. Boron selectivity is achieved by functionalizing pristine anodes (commercial carbon cloth) with a series of boron-selective functional groups, which demonstrate a high affinity for borate ions over competing ions (e.g., chloride) in aqueous solutions. Detailed characterization of the functionalized anodes reveals higher surface area, smaller pore size, and a greater number of surface functional groups, compared with the pristine anode. The electrosorption performance of these functionalized anodes is investigated using a custom-built bipolar membrane (BPM) assisted electrosorption device. Results from the performance tests show that the functionalization methods increase boron selectivity over chloride by up to an order of magnitude compared to the pristine anode. This project also evaluates the long-term stability of the functionalized anodes and energy consumption. Molecular dynamics simulations and nuclear magnetic resonance attribute the selective mechanisms to hydrogen bonding and complexation between boron and functional groups. This study addresses persistent inefficiencies in current boron removal technologies and presents an effective approach for the electrosorption of weak acids and bases.

This work has made substantial contributions to the advancement of selective separation technologies. The findings resulted in four publications in high-impact journals, including Journal of the American Chemical Society, Environmental Science & Technology, and Water Research. Furthermore, five presentations were delivered at international conferences, increasing visibility for the innovative methodologies and discoveries made through this project. It also played a key role in training undergraduate and graduate students, along with several postdoctoral researchers, who are now applying these skills in their professional and academic careers.

abstractText:
The main objective of this project is to study the relation between L-functions and various periods, both automorphic and arithmetic. The L-function is an important object in the modern study of questions in number theory, in particular, solving Diophantine equations like the famous Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture and its generalizations. L-functions are also crucial in the study of representations of transformation groups, which have an important role in physics. The work is expected to provide important new understanding of these relations in higher dimensional cases. The investigator plans to organize workshops related to the project, which will provide students, postdocs, and other researchers in the area substantial opportunities for instruction, discussion, and collaboration.

The scope of this project consists of four parts. In the first part, the investigator will use some new techniques in the study of trace formulas to solve questions concerning the relation between L-functions and automorphic periods -- those periods obtained by integrating automorphic forms along certain subgroups. The second part aims to extend some explicit formulas of automorphic periods, known as the Ichino-Ikeda formula, to more general cases by removing certain assumptions that are usually hard to check. The third part aims to provide unconditional evidence toward the Beilinson-Bloch conjecture on the relation between L-functions and Chow groups, which will generalize parallel results in the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture to higher dimensional cases. In the last part, the investigator plans to adopt a new approach via a relative trace formula to obtain variants of the arithmetic triple product formula concerning the height of certain cycles on a product of three modular elliptic curves.

Intellectual merit

One origin of number theory is to solve polynomial equations over the field Q of rational numbers, i.e., to find Q-points on algebraic varieties over Q. In modern number theory, we want to quantify these points or to investigate their configuration and distribution. A natural extension is to study algebraic cycles, i.e., formal linear combinations of closed subvarieties, on algebraic varieties over fields closely related to Q.   Chow groups are abelian groups of algebraic cycles modulo rational equivalence. Here, rational equivalence identifies algebraic cycles via “defor- mation” along the projective line.

Starting with a polynomial equation y^2=f(x) that defines a curve C. If f(x) is cubic,  there is a natural abelian group law on C and C is an elliptic curve. Moreover, the Birch--Swinnerton-Dyer (BSD) conjecture — one of the most important problems in number theory — equates the rank of C(Q) and the central vanishing order of  the L-function of C.  In the case of vanishing order 1, Gross and Zagier showed that an earlier construction of Heegner using CM points on some modular curves (i.e., moduli spaces of Elliptic curves) actually gives a point in C(Q) of infinite order. The key ingredient is the Gross– Zagier formula that relates  heights of CM points and derivatives of L-functions for modular forms.  This is the most important tool we have for the BSD conjecture. One of the Beilinson--Bloch (BB) conjecture vastly generalizes the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture using Chow groups. The major outcomes of the project are on the BB conjecture, via establishing generalizations of the Gross--Zagier formula in higher dimensions. . 

First, Yifeng Liu (the PI before changing) has accompolished two articles on the BB conjecture  for unitary Shimura varieties, joint with Chao Li. They established  an arithmetic inner product formula, generalizing of the Gross--Zagier formula from a new angle. Second,  Congling Qiu (the PI after changing) has written an article on the higher weight Gross--Zagier formula for  Kuga-Sato varieties over any modular curves.  Third, Congling Qiu (the PI after changing) has written an article about an arithmetic mixed Siegel-Weil formula for unitary Shimura varieties, analogous to the key formula in the work of Gross and Zagier that directly leads to  the Gross--Zagier formula. A direct application of the arithmetic mixed Siegel-Weil formula is a solution to Kudla’s modularity problem for the arithmetic algebraic cycles. 

.Another conjecture of Beilinson--Bloch predicts that the Abel--Jacobi maps from Chow groups to the intermediate Jacobians are injective modulo torsion, i.e., algebraic cycles modulo rational equivalence and torsion can be determined Hodge-theoreticly. Congling Qiu (the PI after changing) has written an article with Wei Zhang about this conjecture for  diagonal cycles on powers of curves. They also have a paper in preparation, when the curves are specialized to Shimura curves (generalizatios of modular curves). It completely solves a complement of Gross--Kudla's conjectural generalizations of the Gross--Zagier formula to triple product of Shimura curves. Finally, Congling Qiu (the PI after changing) has a paper in preparation, solving this conjecture for  CM zero cycles on squares of elliptic curves, and partially for Shimura curves. 

Broader impacts

The research of the PIs are disseminated through respected journals and through conferences, seminars and lectures. Parts of the research are joint works with other mathematicians. Some problems in the research are made into research projects of graduate students. Certain aspects of this research could generate several undergraduate projects. The PIs plan to organize workshops or conferences related to the research, which will provide students, postdocs, and other mathematicians in the area substantial opportunities for instruction, discussion and collaboration.

abstractText:
Why are bats so likely to carry coronaviruses, yet seem little affected by them? Many studies have focused on their immune system, but there is much to learn about the cells viruses attack upon entry. Acute respiratory symptoms, as well as the curious loss of the sense of smell in human patients with COVID-19 hint that cells in the nasal passage are afflicted first. Indeed, cells that produce mucus in the nose, known as goblet cells, have been shown to be “ground zero” for viral entry. Since these cells are also present in bat noses, there must be a difference in how coronaviruses attack goblet cells in bats versus humans. However, virtually nothing is known about immune-related proteins in bat goblet cells. This project proposes a new approach to understand how bats are resistant to respiratory viruses such as those related to SARS-CoV-2. By generating a multi-dimensional study of the anatomy and physiology of the upper respiratory tract —nose and pharynx— of bats, the proposed work will enable researchers to better understand how viruses enter the body and infect or fail to infect their hosts. This project will also allow health agencies around the world to better survey bat populations and prevent future pandemics similar to COVID-19.  In addition, this proposal supports a graduate student and post-doctoral fellow to increase training in STEM fields.  

Researchers supported by this award will test the hypothesis that bats with nasal anatomy similar to humans have a specific composition of the lining of their respiratory tract, evolved to prevent viruses such as SARS-CoV-2, from infecting them. To understand how the lining, or epithelium, is modified in bats compared to humans, this grant will compare the proteins, DNA, and histology of bats to humans and mice. The proposed work will highlight the role of goblet cells, which do not only produce mucus, but also have immune and inflammatory functions, as critical for infection from- versus resistance to viral attack. The team will also integrate layers of data, from 3D imaging to proteomics, to build a complete picture of the inner and outer workings of the upper respiratory tracts of bats. By visualizing the anatomy in high resolution and uncovering which specific proteins are produced by the lining of the bat’s nasal passage, this project will produce the most thorough study of the upper respiratory tracts of bats yet. This will be critical for humanity’s fight against zoonotic viruses, and surveillance of wildlife populations. This RAPID award is made by the Physiological and Structural Systems Cluster in the BIO Division of Integrative Organismal Systems, using funds from the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act.

projectOutComesReport:
The purpose of this award was to visualize and compare the mucus-producing cells inside the noses of bats and determine if bats that circulate coronaviruses demonstrated notable differences, potentially contributing to their ability to harbor respiratory viruses at high rates. The project resul. The most notable finding is that horseshoe bats, major zoonotic hosts of coronaviruses, have undergone dramatic nasal rearrangment to optimize for high-duty frequency echolocation, and their nasopharynx (i.e., throat) has moved forward sealing off the respiratory region of the nose from the olfactory region. As a result, the goblet cells are restricted only to the nasopharynx area, limiting interaction with the olfactory system and potential avenues for infection of more remote tissues. 

This project trained eight undergraduates, two graduate students, and a postdoc. Numerous of these undergraduates have moved onto graduate school. The postdoc is now an Assistant Professor in a research-focused position. It also resulted in an NSF Research Experience for Post-Baccalaureate Students (REPS) fellowship that trained a recent graduate in molecular and histological methods. This trainee is now working as a research assistant in the pathology department of a hospital.  

The results were dissemminated at several international conference procedings Infectious Diseases of Bats in Fort Collins, CO and the Evolution Conferences. Many of these presentations were given by undergraduates and the post-baccalaureate trained on this grant. The project resulted in six peer-reviewed manuscripts, several with student co-authors. Several more outcomes are in preparation for peer-reviewed publication.

abstractText:
The conversion of carbon dioxide (CO2) into more valuable compounds is an important goal due to the potential of this waste product as a readily available, sustainable, non-toxic, and inexpensive chemical feedstock. Catalysts based on transition metals, such as nickel or palladium, show promise speeding up the reactions of carbon dioxide so that they are practical, but improvements in efficiency are required for further implementation. In this project, Dr. Hazari of Yale University is developing an understanding of how carbon dioxide interacts with a variety of transition metal complexes using both experimental and computational techniques. This knowledge is crucial for the design of improved systems for carbon dioxide utilization as it will provide information on how to modify the catalyst as well as how to improve the conditions under which reactions are performed (temperature, pressure, etc.). This research has potential to increased selectivity so that only desired products are formed.  The research is complemented by Dr. Hazari’s involvement in a series of outreach activities related to carbon dioxide utilization.  These activities focus on students from underrepresented minorities in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) disciplines. The activities include a one week summer program on energy for high school students in the New Haven area and opportunities for undergraduates to perform research in Dr. Hazari’s laboratory. 

With funding from the Chemical Structure, Dynamics, and Mechanisms B (CSDM-B) Program of the Chemistry Division, Dr. Hazari from Yale University is developing a fundamental understanding of the insertion of carbon dioxide into late-transition metal bonds. This research provides guidance about the design of catalysts and optimization of reaction conditions for processes involving carbon dioxide utilization. Specifically, the rates of carbon dioxide insertion into Group 10 pincer-supported transition metal hydrides, hydroxides, alkyls, and aryls are being measured. Factors that are being probed include the effects of the metal center, ancillary ligand, solvent, and additives, such as Lewis acids, on the kinetics of carbon dioxide insertion. A major focus is the development of scaling relationships that correlate the rate of carbon dioxide insertion into a metal hydride (a kinetic property), with the hydricity of transition metal hydrides, a thermodynamic property. This enables the evaluation of hypotheses relating to whether secondary coordination sphere effects such as hydrogen bonding or electrostatic effects that stabilize the transition state for carbon dioxide insertion. Density Functional Theory calculations are carried out in parallel with the experimental work and probe the structure of the transition states, determine the geometries of unstable intermediates, and measure hydricity.

projectOutComesReport:
The goal of this project was to understand the pathways through which carbon dioxide interacts with different transition metal complexes and how the reaction environment influences these pathways. These studies are important as they could guide the development of systems for the conversion of carbon dioxide into more valuable products, such as fuels. In one thrust, the PI's group explored the reaction of nickel and palladium complexes with carbon dioxide. In particular, they explored reactions that formed new carbon-carbon bonds from carbon dioxide, which are directly relevant to fuel formation. To complete these studies, they used a new supporting environment around the palladium and nickel complexes and investigated the reaction using computational techniques. They established a specific set of guidelines for predicting which supporting environments around the metal center promote reactions with carbon dioxide. Two detailed papers describing the work in this thrust were published in peer-reviewed journals.

In a related thrust, the effect of different solvents on the formation of C-H bonds from the reaction of rhenium complexes with carbon dioxide was explored. Using both experimental and theoretical methods, a model was developed to predict the effect of solvent on these reactions. It was discovered that the general principles elucidated for understanding the reactions of rhenium complexes with carbon dioxide, could also be applied to organic reactions that are used for the synthesis of pharmaceuticals and materials. As such, the initial model was far more general and powerful than initially expected. Four papers were published in relation to this work.

The scientific research performed as part of this award was complemented by Dr. Hazari's involvement in a series of outreach activities related to catalysis and carbon dioxide utilization. These activities catered to students from underrepresented minorities in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) disciplines. They included twice hosting an activity called 'The Wonderful World of Chemistry – A Magic Show'. In this event, the PI's group educated local school students about chemistry through a one-hour lecture that included a series of demonstrations, as well as educational content. Additionally, the PI's group twice participated in the Yale Summer Scholars Program, which hosts local high school students on campus. On one occasion, the PI's group gave five interactive lectures on alternative energy and catalysis, while on another occasion the PI delivered a ninety-minute lecture. Finally, the PI's group hosted two undergraduate researchers who worked in the research laboratories over summer and assisted with their professional development.

abstractText:
Biochar is a carbon-rich solid byproduct of thermochemical biomass conversions. It has potential applications in food, energy, and water systems. This project aims to advance potential biochar applications by (1) using artificial intelligence (machine learning) approaches to predict process data and life cycle assessment (LCA) of various combinations of biomass feedstocks, conversion pathways, and applications of biochar; (2) building an integrated framework for modeling and analysis of biochar systems in the food-energy-water (FEW) nexus; and (3) demonstrating the framework through real-world case studies in different geographic, temporal, and socioeconomic contexts. The educational and outreach objectives include (1) attracting underrepresented students to STEM fields by developing a multimedia package for FEW and biochar sustainability; (2) developing both in-class and online courses and providing training and professional development opportunities to integrate research and education activities for undergraduate and graduate students; (3) developing an international network of scholars for FEW, biochar sustainability, and interdisciplinary research communities with a long-term goal of forming an international research and education program.

This project targets bridging knowledge gaps for biochar production and effective applications in enhancing FEW sustainability by integrating LCA, technico-economic analysis (TEA), Geographic Information System (GIS), machine learning, and dynamic modeling. Understanding the impacts of using various biomass substrates for different biochar applications on the environment, economics, and communities will lay a foundation for the further design and implementation of large-scale biochar systems under different socioeconomic, climate change, and resource limiting conditions. Integration of advanced modeling tools including LCA, GIS, and machine learning that are commonly used in different disciplines is an important feature of the approach. Through integration of advanced modeling methods from engineering, environmental science, natural science, and data science, this project seeks to demonstrate how transdisciplinary research can create improved societal outcomes.

projectOutComesReport:
Biochar, a carbon-rich product of thermochemical biomass conversions, has gained significant interest due to its potential applications in food, energy, and water systems while serving as a nature-based method for carbon sequestration. However, challenges remain in optimizing its production and application to maximize environmental benefits and economic viability. This project aimed to address these challenges by bridging fundamental knowledge gaps through the integration of machine learning, life cycle assessment (LCA), techno-economic analysis (TEA), Geographic Information System (GIS) modeling, and dynamic modeling.

Using our integrated framework, we assessed the conversion of urban tree waste into biochar in various U.S. cities, revealing its substantial potential in reducing greenhouse gases (GHG) and eutrophication impacts. Importantly, we identified that the degree of these benefits varies significantly by location, highlighting the need for region-specific strategies.

We compiled global datasets for biochar production from various biomass sources and their application as a soil amendment. We assessed life cycle environmental impacts of biochar across multiple regions and contexts. This assessment included evaluating the effectiveness of biochar in combination with other nature-based solutions, such as afforestation/reforestation on marginal land and the use of long-lived wood products. Our findings indicated that integrating biochar with these solutions could deliver significant long-term GHG mitigation benefits, although short-term impacts depend on forest management strategies. In addition to soil amendment, our analysis of various biochar applications identified gaps in using machine learning for biochar systems. We proposed a workflow for future machine learning studies for biochar and other carbonaceous materials in the water and agriculture sectors.

Our analysis, which incorporates both environmental and economic aspects, offered unique insights into the spatial variations of not only GHG mitigation but also economic returns from landowner perspectives. We assessed how different ecological factors, future climate, and resource-limiting conditions may have affected the landowner decisions at different regions, demonstrating the powerful use of our integrated modeling framework to support region-specific decision making from both environmental and economic sustainability perspectives.

Furthermore, we explored the co-production of biochar with bioenergy, particularly from forest residues, which are abundant in the U.S. Our analyses demonstrated the critical role of biochar end-uses in affecting the economic feasibility and environmental impact of these systems. Our integration of soil carbon modeling into LCA highlighted the significant role of soil organic carbon changes in the life cycle emissions of bioenergy-biochar systems. This emphasizes the need to consider ecosystem dynamics for future LCA, especially when used for biochar project evaluation, policymaking, and resource management.

Our findings have been widely disseminated through conferences, seminars, and 15 peer-reviewed journal articles. We have provided open access to data generated from this project to support future biochar research. The project has also established an international network of scholars by engaging with organizations such as the American Institute of Chemical Engineers and the International Society for Industrial Ecology.

Our research results have been integrated into education via courses on life cycle assessment and industrial ecology at Yale and NC State University, training over 200 graduate and undergraduate students. For outreach, we have developed multimedia educational materials to engage middle and high school students and teachers in North Carolina, aiming to increase student interest in STEM fields. This project has supported 3 postdoctoral researchers, 3 PhD students, and multiple master’s students by providing research and professional development opportunities. One postdoctoral researcher from this project successfully obtained a tenure-track assistant professor position.

The results from this project enhance our understanding of the environmental and economic implications of biochar production and applications in various local contexts. That advanced knowledge can guide strategies for developing sustainable biochar systems to maximize sustainability benefits from local to global scales. This project has also advanced fundamental LCA methods by improving the modeling capacity of spatially and temporally dynamic systems. These methodological improvements extend beyond biochar and can be applied in other sectors such as chemical production, transportation, and buildings. The integration of modeling tools from different fields, such as industrial ecology, chemical engineering, economics, environmental science, and data science, demonstrates the potential of transdisciplinary research to improve environmental and societal benefits.

abstractText:
Over billions of years of Earth history, continents have drifted across the globe, periodically assembling into supercontinents.  Pangea was the most recent of these: a single landmass that joined the Americas to Europe and Africa, prior to spreading of the Atlantic Ocean.  Pangea was likely preceded by more ancient supercontinents named Rodinia (about 900 million years ago) and Nuna (about 1.5 billion years ago), both existing within the “Proterozoic” time interval of primordial life.  Although these supercontinents have names, their exact arrangements of continental fragments remain uncertain.  Regardless, geologists are beginning to speculate on whether the supercontinental transitions generally have an accordion-like pattern of motion (imagine a future for the Americas reversing their course and drifting eastward to close the Atlantic Ocean and re-collide with Europe and Africa), or whether continents circumnavigate the globe (imagine the Americas continuing to drift westward to close the Pacific Ocean and collide with eastern Asia and Australia, thus turning the old supercontinent “inside-out”).  These ideas help shape our view of Earth’s evolving deep interior over billions of years, and also give geographical context to the formation of mineral deposits, ancient climate records, and biological evolution at the longest timescales. This project uses two complementary methods of laboratory measurement to determine how the continents have moved across the Earth’s surface: paleomagnetism—the ancient record of the geomagnetic field that is recorded by rocks; and the isotopic dating of the age of rocks using the radioactive decay of uranium to lead.  The project focuses on the least well-understood continental fragment in the Nuna and Rodinia supercontinental landmasses:  the West African craton. Within West Africa, particularly the Anti-Atlas Mountains of Morocco, recent advances of geological understanding provide an opportunity to apply the two methods to ancient volcanic rock systems (“mafic dikes”) of a variety of ages, to produce more accurate reconstructions of the Nuna and Rodinia landmasses and to discover the patterns of Earth’s supercontinental transitions.  The project will involve collection of rock samples in the field, laboratory analyses on those specimens, and publication of results in peer-reviewed journals. In addition to the scientific goals of the project, important societal outcomes associated with this project include training the next generation of Earth scientists in an important science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) discipline; incorporation of the project’s results into public museum displays; and development of educational modules with K-12 public school teachers.

Uncertainties in the configurations of supercontinents Nuna and Rodinia currently permit either of two end-member views on long-term global geodynamics: whether supercontinents tend to revert to prior configurations, or turn “inside-out.”  It is also possible that they have alternated between those two patterns in time.  West Africa's paleogeography is the least constrained of all major Precambrian cratons, and its previously hypothesized placement either within the middle of pre-Pangean supercontinents or along their periphery is crucial to the aforementioned debate.  This project seeks to conduct an integrated paleomagnetic and geochronological study of mafic dike swarms in Precambrian inliers of the Anti-Atlas Mountains, Morocco.  High-quality and precisely dated paleomagnetic poles obtained from this study will fill a notable gap in the tectonic and kinematic history of West Africa and neighboring blocks in Nuna and Rodinia, and provide essential ground-truth to the debate on supercontinental transitional styles.

abstractText:
Given the pivotal role of data and cyberinfrastructure (CI) in scientific discovery and teaching, it is essential that all small and mid-sized institutions be empowered to fully exploit them. Access to physical infrastructure is certainly required, but researchers also need access to “Research Computing Facilitators” (RCFs) possessing the mix of technical knowledge and interpersonal skills required to help them use CI resources effectively. This poses challenges for smaller institutions, since RCFs are in short supply and are difficult to recruit and retain. Moreover, institutions can often afford only one or two, making it challenging to support diverse scientific disciplines.
 
This project is developing a sustainable distributed approach to address these challenges in six Eastern states, facilitated by the Eastern Regional Network, a nascent, but growing collaboration among this project’s seven anchor institutions, other institutions in the Eastern US, and the area’s regional network providers. The project strategy has two principal legs: (1) expanding the RCF talent pipeline by engaging students at smaller institutions in nearly 70 project-based mentored experiential learning opportunities; and (2) developing a regional RCF pool providing CI facilitation across institutional and geographic boundaries.
 
Success of this project directly enhances scientific research at smaller institutions. The regional RCF pool enables researchers to access appropriate expertise without the costs and delays of building an institutional RCF team. The experiential training approach exposes a relatively large, diverse group of students to the RCF profession, yielding opportunities to encourage trainees, especially in underrepresented groups, to pursue RCF careers.

projectOutComesReport:
Advanced cyberinfrastructure (CI) is essential to modern scientific discovery. To succeed, researchers must be equipped to fully utilize CI. Access to physical infrastructure is essential but insufficient. Researchers also need human resources (“research computing facilitators” or RCFs) who possess both technical expertise and the interpersonal skills to work effectively with them. At most large institutions, adequate numbers of RCFs may be available, but at smaller institutions, RCFs are often in short supply and are generally difficult to hire and retain. This places researchers at such schools at a significant disadvantage. 

The CAREERS program investigated ways to provide facilitation services to small and mid-size schools in six states using a two-pronged strategy: 

  1. Expand the RCF talent pipeline by engaging students in mentored experiential learning opportunities; and

  2. Develop infrastructure and tools to support distributed pools of RCFs that could provide shared facilitation services across institutional and geographic boundaries.

Outcome 1: Expanding the RCF Pipeline

The experiential learning opportunities offered by CAREERS were based on a project workflow developed by the Northeast Cyberteam in a previous NSF program. CAREERS significantly expanded and automated the workflow to scale to many participants, large geographic regions, and a broad range of research disciplines and institutions. The workflow follows a structured sequence:

  1. Steering committee members and others recruit researchers with projects needing facilitation;

  2. Projects are advertised on the CAREERS portal, and students and mentors are notified of opportunities; 

  3. Students and mentors express interest in projects via the portal; and

  4. CAREERS leadership team utilizes portal matchmaking capabilities to match mentors to students and researchers.

Throughout the program, we held monthly all-hands meetings for CAREERS participants, typically with 25-30 attendees. For each project, students gave two talks: a “launch presentation,” shortly after the project began, and a “wrap presentation” after project completion. These presentations taught students how to speak to technical groups and answer questions from researchers, RCFs, and other students. In between these presentations, students gave brief oral summaries (“elevator pitches”) at each meeting describing project status and activities, and highlighting technical issues so that others present might be able to assist. 

Experiential learning projects helped expand the pipeline of potential RCFs. In aggregate, 68 projects were completed during the CAREERS program, and ~350 individuals joined our portal, with ~190 of them participating actively in projects. Projects provided meaningful work experiences and demonstrated how RCFs could facilitate research projects, even without much domain-specific expertise. Students came away with an understanding of the importance of advanced research computing and of the value of RCFs. Several indicated interest in facilitation as a potential career option.

Outcome 2: Sustainability for Training Activities

Trainees participating in CAREERS projects received monetary participant stipends to encourage active engagement throughout their 3-6 month project commitments. These stipends comprised a significant portion of the CAREERS budget. In year 4, we began to explore sustainability strategies for the program, eventually settling on an approach using academic credits associated with internships and capstone projects as currency, instead of monetary stipends. As before, researchers could propose projects via the CAREERS portal, and interested RCF students, even those from different institutions, could sign up. Not surprisingly, distributed multi-institution capstone projects do require attentive program management and more careful planning and time than projects within a single department or institution. However, with sufficient flexibility and commitment, all involved can have a highly rewarding experience. Based on the pilots we ran, we regard this model as a viable path to sustainability for experiential training programs like CAREERS, factoring in program management and portal maintenance costs.

Outcome 3: Infrastructure and Tools for the CI Community

Another important outcome of the CAREERS project is the ConnectCI Community Management Platform. The CAREERS portal was modeled after one created for the Northeast Cyberteam. Recognizing a need for similar portals across the CI community, the CAREERS portal team developed a replicable portal architecture instead of a one-off clone of the existing site. They separated functions that were program-specific from sharable infrastructure such as the knowledge base and the personnel directory. The infrastructure was branded “ConnectCI,” and each participating program was given independent portal “views” that utilized the shared infrastructure but provided independent program-specific information. ConnectCI has subsequently been used to develop portals for various NSF-funded programs including ACCESS Support, the Campus Champions, Cyberinfrastructure Community-Wide Mentorship Network and Open OnDemand, and additional portals are in the pipeline. Each portal is hosted on ConnectCI, but runs independently of the others, sharing a common knowledge base, personnel directory, event and announcement capabilities, and affinity groups. All elements are indexed using a common vocabulary of CI terms (the “tag taxonomy”), which is used by search engines to deliver useful content from the shared database. CAREERS’s seminal investment in ConnectCI enabled the extensive, collective capability offered to the CI community through these ConnectCI-based portals.

abstractText:
The theory of surfaces interacts deeply with all parts of mathematics. The confluence of topology, geometry, group theory, complex analysis and dynamics in dimension two is a constant source of rich structure and influences many fields both directly and by analogy. Because surfaces are simple and flexible, they admit large parameter spaces of shapes. The study of these spaces is useful directly in topology and geometry in all dimensions.  The PI will explore the geometry of the space of shapes of a surface, and the relationships between flows within this more abstract space and the ways in which three-dimensional structures are built out of families of two-dimensional structures. By way of analogy, ideas in two and three dimensions have also inspired powerful techniques in allied fields such as geometric group theory and dynamics. Part of the PI's work will explore some of these connections. Graduate students funded by the grant will, in addition to their research work, be trained in mathematics education and outreach, preparing them for contributions to society through higher education and other leadership roles. Additional activities of the PI and his students and collaborators will include public educational activities for local school children and their families, bringing cutting-edge mathematical knowledge to the greater New Haven community.

The PI plans to study a number of aspects of the Weil-Petersson geometry of the Teichmuller space of a surface, and its connections to the theory of 3-manifolds and more broadly to group actions in other settings.  Recent work of the PI and coauthors has shed some new light on the study of the geodesic flow of the Weil-Petersson metric on Teichmuller space, and its connection to the structure of fibered 3-manifolds. With these results in mind, the PI plans a more detailed study of the coarse structure of the Teichmuller space as made visible by the cubical and metric structure of its asymptotic cone. This point of view suggests interesting questions about minimal surfaces in the Teichmuller space, and avenues toward resolving the visibility problem for the WP geodesic flow. New connections of Weil-Petersson geometry to the structure of fibered 3-manifolds and Thurston's norm on homology hint at deeper structure which the PI plans to investigate.  In the theory of 3-manifolds, the deep interaction between decompositions along surfaces, structure of curve complexes and mapping class groups, and hyperbolic geometry continues to provide challenging questions. The PI will work on developing a more complete theory for canonical decompositions of 3-manifolds, focusing on the interactions of Heegaard splittings, fibrations and subsurface projections. He will study the problem of finding uniform models for hyperbolic manifolds and obtaining a priori bounds on skinning maps. The setting of Heegaard splittings and handlebodies connects to a new approach on character varieties of free groups, via a technique of graph folding in hyperbolic space.  Additional projects (some with students) include the study of hierarchically hyperbolic spaces, mapping class groups of infinite-type surfaces, and relations between hyperbolic earthquakes and the Teichmuller horocyclic flow.

abstractText:
Non-Technical Abstract
The origin of electrical resistance in simple metals is well-described by a model in which electrons behave like independent billiard balls colliding within the material, and losing energy in the process. On the other hand, in superconducting quantum materials many electrons behave collectively to create a state where electric current can flow without energy loss. In many cases, these quantum materials may feature enhanced properties that defy our conventional knowledge, and could be key to the future of clean energy transmission and other everyday technologies. However, as one tries to enhance superconductivity, other phenomena, including ordered states, appear as well. The fundamental roadblock is to understand how these additional intertwined orders are detrimental or helpful to the superconductivity. This project uses complementary scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, a tool that visualizes the electrons in the sub-nanoscale, and resonant x-ray scattering to investigate the role of intertwined orders in superconducting quantum materials, while manipulating the materials using a variety of conditions like external field or temperature. This project also uses online tools for the broader dissemination of knowledge. Several online video modules, featuring undergraduate and graduate students, demonstrate and explain the advanced laboratory techniques related to this project. This project also targets the inclusion of underrepresented minorities through the development of teaching modules for the Mentorships for Undergraduate Research Participants in the Physical and Mathematical Sciences program at UC Davis.

Technical Abstract
Understanding how quantum materials develop collective electronic phenomena is one of the biggest challenges facing condensed matter physicists today. The key to unlocking quantum materials comes from understanding how multiple phases are intrinsically intertwined and cannot exist alone. In quantum materials, superconductivity may intertwine with phases where electrons self-organize into unusual patterns (density waves) or into states where the x and y directions become nonequivalent for electrons in an otherwise square crystal (nematic order). This project investigates the role of intertwined orders in unconventional superconductors, focusing on two important cases : (i) studies of  the relationship between density-wave order, magnetism and superconductivity in the Ce-based 115 family of heavy-fermion superconductors using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy (STM/S) and resonant x-ray scattering techniques; and (ii) studies of superconducting and nematic orders in Fe-based superconductors by integrating STM/S and uniaxial strain to control the nematic order. Through these activities, this research ultimately targets the direct visualization of a pair-density-wave state in a heavy fermion superconductor and the switchable control of superconductivity by crystal deformation of Fe-based superconductors. Finally, the development of a new methodology to study nematic order via the integration of uniaxial strain to STM/S will have significant impact on the study of other quantum materials.

projectOutComesReport:
In superconducting quantum materials, electrons form a macroscopic quantum state below a critical temperature, allowing electric current to flow without energy loss. These materials, with properties such as high critical temperatures, offer potential advances in clean energy transmission and other technologies. However, enhancing superconductivity often encounters intertwined quantum ordering phenomena. Understanding if these orders aid or hinder superconductivity is a key challenge. This project used techniques like scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, and resonant x-ray scattering to study these phases and their effects on superconductivity.

The flagship scientific finding of this project is described in our publication: Nature Physics 21, 89–96 (2025). In this study, we investigated the Fe-based superconductor system Fe(Se,S) and explored the relationship between dynamic fluctuations of nematic order and superconductivity. Over the past 15 years, unconventional superconductivity in Fe-based materials has been extensively studied. Electronic nematicity, a quantum state of matter where rotational symmetry is broken, was proposed 25 years ago and is prominent in Fe-based superconductors. Although long-range nematic order can either compete with or enhance superconductivity, the impact of nematic fluctuations on the mechanisms of superconducting pairing remained unresolved. Understanding how nematicity influences superconductivity, and whether nematic fluctuations alone can induce superconductivity, are critical questions in the field.

Our study focused on Fe(Se,S) with a composition of 81% Se atoms and 19% S atoms, which optimizes the material (near a nematic quantum critical point) for exhibiting the novel superconducting mechanism where Cooper pairs are mediated by nematic fluctuations. However, detecting the signature of this state has been challenging. The key theoretically predicted signature was the anisotropy of the superconducting gap in momentum space. Accurate determination of this signature requires measurements at temperatures below 1 K, a condition under which traditional techniques such as angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) face difficulties.

To overcome these challenges, we employed scanning tunneling spectroscopy (STS), which provided the necessary low temperature and high energy resolution to resolve the superconducting gap structure. We determined the momentum structure of the superconducting gap near the center of the Brillouin zone in Fe(Se,S) from quasiparticle interference (QPI) signals, close to the quantum critical point, finding it to be anisotropic and nearly nodal. The gap minima occur in a direction rotated by 45 degrees with respect to the Fe-Fe direction, distinct from the usual isotropic gaps due to spin-mediated mechanisms. Altogether this evidence provided strong evidence for the existence of superconductivity mediated by nematic fluctuations.

Related to this work, we also undertook several complementary studies to deepen our understanding of the properties of Fe-based superconductors: (i) We investigated the normal state band structure of tetragonal Fe(Se,S). Through this study, we developed new methods for analyzing quasiparticle interference (QPI) patterns, which revealed a pronounced pattern of short-range two-fold symmetric stripe patterns in nanosized domains [npj Quantum Materials 8, Article number: 60 (2023)]. (ii) To further understand the superconductivity mediated by nematic fluctuations, we performed careful simulations of the QPI signal. In doing so, we developed a novel analysis method called intermediate band analysis [Phys. Rev. B 111, 235148 2025].

Another critical aspect of intertwined orders involves the coexistence of nematicity, charge order, and superconductivity in cuprate high-temperature superconductors. Utilizing techniques adapted for controlling nematicity in Fe-based superconductors, this project explored the intertwined nematicity and charge order in cuprates [Phys. Rev. Res. 3, L022004 (2021)]. We aimed to understand how dynamic fluctuations of these orders influence superconductivity and strange metal behavior. Employing resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS), we developed a phonon-tracking methodology, revealing low-energy quasi-circular charge order correlations [Science Advances 9 (29), eadg3710 (2023)]. Additionally, our polarimetric RIXS (pol-RIXS) in the soft x-ray regime achieved high-resolution two-phonon features [Physical Review B 109 (12), 125126 (2024)]. The insights gained supported experimental [Science 376 (6595), 860-864] and theoretical [Physical Review B 108 (19), 195141 (2023)] studies with collaborators, and many results were summarized in a review paper [Frontiers in Electronic Materials 4, 1473324 (2024)].

This project also contributed to several broader impacts goals. It supported three physics PhD graduate students, two of whom have graduated and one who is expected to graduate in 2026. All students gained significant skills in quantum research, published first-author manuscripts, and are continuing or planning to continue in quantum research, in both industry and academia. We also developed three in-person outreach modules for the Yale Pathways to Science program, engaging approximately 40 high school students, and conducted one virtual event during the pandemic. The events were: Quantum mechanics and quantum tunnelling: lecture and virtual tour with atomic microscope (2021), Visualizing atoms with quantum tunneling (2022), How Do You See Very Small Things With Physics - Microscopy and Diffraction (2024), and Hello Quantum World! (2025).
